NEW YORK. April Big Clyde
Lovelette of Kansas, a member of
the United States Olympic basket
ball team, against whom questions
of professionalism has been raised,
has been cleared by a special COM
mittee of the AAU.


Two professional basketball
teams had intimated they had Of
fered Lovelette as much as $50, 900
to turn pro, but that he had turned
down these offers to play with
the Phillips Petroleum, Corp. anna
teur team. The implication was
that their offers had been met or
topped.


The special committee investi-
eating the matter heard witnesses
from the Phillips Corp. and also
from the Caterpillar Tractor Co..
another big sponsor Of amateur
basketball. The gist of their testi-
mony was that their basketball
players also were full-time en-
ployes, and that they received no
more salary than others doing the
same type Of work.


The Phillips witness admitted
his company was interested in
fielding a representative basket
ball team, but that every player
was required to render efficient
service for the salary paid him.
OF all the players who have rep
resented Phillips on the court, 80
per cent still are with the COM
pany and many Of them are among
the higher officers, he said.


The testimony from the Cater
pillar Co. was similar. The COM
mittee's four-page report con-
cluded with the statement that
there was no evidence that would
reflect upon the amateur status of
any of the Olympic basketball
players.

assistance was delivered to the

The delay in Sweden's reply is
because Premier Tage Erlander is
attending Socialist international
meeting in Milan, Italy, and For

What this country needs is a return
to the days of the brass spittoon, the
true symbol of hard-headed, hard
thinking, hard-fsted Americanism.
When spittoons were taken away the
average American turned to cigarettes
and jabber. Nowadays every time two
or more people meet on the street. at
the Office, in the workshop, or elsewhere.
out come the cigarettes and the yak-yak
starts. People have forgotten the art of
listening and thinking. Back in the days
when hard-headed economic and social
policies were formed and which have
been the backbone of this country'S
progress, people were different. Instead
of the liberated conglomeration of
chain smokers yak-yakking at each
other. man was calm, reflective and
thoughtful. When man has medium
sized hunk of chewing tobacco in his
cheek he becomes relaxed and profound.
When two people met in the old days,
one talked while the other chewed and
listened; then both chewed while and
reflected; then the other spit and talked
a while. The result was thoughtful
and productive conversation. Andy
Jackson and Abe Lincoln did not emerge
as presidential candidates from smoke
filled rooms, but from rooms which
tinkled with the liquid chime of Oft
used cuspidors. So let's go back, before
it's too late, to the day of the brass
Spittoon. James Francis.

A strict new system for keeping
Americas vital strategic exports
out of Communist hands goes into
effect october 20.


The Commerce Department an
nounced yesterday that the United
States, Canada and 10 Western
European countries have agreed
to put 1863 important materials
and manufactures under much
tighter control.


These items include anything
useful in atomic energy produc-
ton, almost all machine tools. 10
comotiveS and much railway

tools. much oil well drilling equip

iron and steel scrap, most radio
and radar equipment and others.


In order to keep these products
from trickling through the Iron
Curtain to Russia or its satellites.
the new agreement requires that
their export will be permitted only
when the foreign buyer certifies to
his government that the good will
not be sold to another country
without official permission.


Must Send Original.


The United States exporter
must send the original of this
certification to the Commerce
Department with his application
for export permits.


For example. if a French buyer
wants to purchase locomotive
from an American firm, he first
must promise his government
and sign a certificate-that the
locomotive will not be sold out
side France to another country
unless the French government
approves.


Then, the American locomotive
exporter must present this certif1-
cate to the Commerce Depart
ment. If the situation seem to
justify, the Department will give
the American seller permission to
go ahead with the deal.


Nations in System.


Countries cooperating with the
United States and Canada are
Belgium, Denmark. France, Italy.
Luxembourg, the Netherlands,
Norway, Portugal. the Ur<e6
Kingdom and Western Germany.
The agreement was reached
after the United States and
Canada conducted separate but
similar negotiations with the 10I
nations. There are no export con-
trolls between the United States
and Canada.


The 1853 items going under the
new clamp-down were selected
from a master list of 1,712 pro-
ducts considered more or less
strategic by this country.


These 1,712 products now may
be exported after the foreign i'm
porter has signed a statement
without government certifica-
tion-that the strategic goods will
not be passed on to another coun-
try.

|emplacemehts.

hill fighting on the east coast the

NEW YORK, Dec. 25.-Now Is
the time when next years al
manacS come bursting out like
spring flowers.


In this age of newspapers, radio.
television and movies the little
paper-backed books are still the
daily guides Of millions. They
hang by the cookstove in many
farmhouse kitchens and lie on
many Park avenue desks.


Industry uses them. too. Cen
eral Motors distributes one al
manac to its employees. The Bell
Telephone System prints and dis
tributes another for its companies
to give away.


Many Almanacs.


Nobody knows how many al
manacs roll off the country's
presses every year, but there are
far more than most people think.
The Old Farmers Almanac, the
Farmers Almanac. the National
Almanac, the New England Al
manac and Farmers Friend. the
World Almanac and Information
Please Almanac are among them.


Some kept the style and layout
that date from their . founding
days, more than $50 years ago
Others have a modern streamlined
makeup. Their content varies just
as much. Many interlard weather
predictions with puzzles, philoso-
ply, jokes, recipes and beauty
hints. The World Almanac con-
centrates on historical and factual
data.


Most devotees value their alma
macs for help in their daily lives.
Many consult them for the time
of sunrise, sunset, weather hints
and tides before they plan a days
work, a weekend jaunt or a fish
ing trip. Farmers check for infor-
nation on killing frosts and when
to put new roof on the barn.
Their wives confer with the alma
nae before they plant flowers or
pick the cucumbers for picking.
Some sports promoters check the
almanac before fixing the date OF a
big outdoor sports event. Hostesses
consult them before a garden party
or wedding.


% par Cent Cnrrect


Most people don't keep close
check on the almanac'S accuracy
in weather predictions, but the
city clerk in Providence, R. l.,
made a year-long observation of
one famous almanac's predictions
some years ago. He reported them
33 per cent correct. During the
some IL months the Weather Bu-
reau's day-to-day forecast was
verified in 35 per cent of its
prophecies.


Almanacs have played a dra-
matte part in some lives. Abraham
Lincoln is said to have won a
murder case by quoting the al
manac to prove that the moon
was low at a certain hour on a
certain night. A court witness
had claimed that it was high and
that he had recognized man in
its full bright light.


Since the first almanacs were
printed centuries ago on coarse
rag paper with woodcut illustra-
tions, many countries have pro-
duced many versions. For years
the Chinese moon almanac con-
stituted a guide to millions of
Chinese peasants in marrying off
their children. burying their dead,
paying their debts and shearing
their hair. England and Germany
also produced famous almanacs.


Poor Richard.


The paper backed weather
prophets began to appear in this
country nearly 100 years before
the colonies became the United
States. The most famous was
Benjamin's Poor Richards AL
manac.


Old settlers tell an entertaining
tale about one of these early al
manacs. While the new edition
was being set up a printers helper
asked the editor what weather he
should note for July 13. The busy
editor impatiently replied: ANY
thing. anything" The boy set up
the July 13 weather prediction as
rain. snow and hail"


The payoff came July 13, when
1t did rain, snow and hail.

Formation of three-State Republican con-
vention alliance involving Maryland, Michigan
and nsylvania-rumored but not yet accom-
plished-could prove a decisive element in the
contest between General Eisenhower and Senator
Taft.


Between them, these States command total
Of 140 convention votes, Of which approximately
100 are currently uncommitted and considered
to be safely in the control of State leaders. At
this point both Governor Fine of Pennsylvania
and National Committeeman Summerfield of
Michigan have expressed no preference between
the two top presidential aspirants while Governor
McKeldin of Maryland has indicated leaning
toward the general.


Both candidates already are working hard
for the three States delegations. General Eisen-
hover, who overwhelmed the Ohio Senator in
the Pennsylvania preference primary, has con-
ferred with Governor Fine this week and enter
tains the entire Pennsylvania delegation at his
Gettysburg farm today Tomorrow he goes into
Michigan for major speech at Detroit. Gov
ernor McKeldin visited with him in New York
few days ago. Senator Taft has meeting sched-
uled later with Governor Fine and is still in
position to make bargain in the other two
States.


From the standpoint of the State leaders
the reported alliance would carry substantial
benefit With the power to throw the nomination
to whichever candidate is their choice, they would
be the band-wagon drivers-in position to COM
mand high political price, both in prediction
local campaign assistance and in post-election
favors if the Republican ticket should win in
November. From party standpoint such COM
bination might also be beneficial in averting
drawn-out and increasingly bitter convention
split, possibility which has worried many Re-
publican supporters and might leave scars which
could badly damage or even destroy the prospects
of November victory.

The goal, then considered barely

Budget cutting by the United

blamed in some quarters.

goal would be difficult to reach

American assistance.

ident Truman's 81 billion foreign

holdover funds were ample and

doing enough for themselves.

an active campaign issue, al
though both candidates, Republic

generally supported the admins
tration policy Of helping to rearm
Western Europe.

A presidential veto was predicted

The bill, passed Thursday by a

Truman. for the Senate Commerce

Those against the measure fear
it may be added in the Senate to a
major appropriation bill. This
would circumvent the Commerce
Committee and make q veto din

Celler Sees Veto.


Chairman Celler Of the House
Judiciary Committee, who led the
House opposition, said the bill
certainly will be vetoed" If it
reaches the President.


Those favoring the bill claim its
main objective is to protect small
business from unfair trade prac-
tices of some large operators.
The District of Columbia and all
the States except Missouri. Texas
and Vermont have trade laws
whose enforcement would be
sanctioned by the House-passed
bill.


These laws previously had been
enforced by the States against all
sellers of goods covered by fair
trade agreements, if any seller in
the State had signed pricing
agreement with the manufacturer
or distributor.
A recent Supreme Court ruling
held that the State laws could not
be enforced against dealers who
didn't sign the agreements.
/ Bill Circumvents Ruling.


The House bill gets around this
ruling and says it is all right for
State laws to permit damage suits
against dealers who sell brand
name articles at prices lower than
are provided for in agreements
with other dealers.


The Budget Bureau opposed the
bill when it was before House
committee.


The Federal Trade Commission
also opposed it. Chairman James
M. Mead said its effect would be
to permit price-f fixing by private

, Commerce Department. through

Dr. Isador Lubin, United States representa-
tive on the United Nations Economic and
Financial Committee, has directed some en-
barrassing and provocative questions at Soviet
Russia and some of its satellites.


Speaking directly to the delegates from these
countries, DR.. Lubin challenged them to explain
the paradox wherein Polish and Czechoslovakian
boasts of increased national production and
strengthened economic and political independ-
ence are paralleled by new and more strict
ratibning measures and open complaints OF
shortages in many commodities The Polish
case is particularly puzzling in view OF that
country's net reduction in population since the
prewar period while it has acquired the rich
agricultural lands of what was formerly part OF
East Germany and the coal and industrial
resources of SIesia.


The implication of DR.. Lubins questioning
was that the "selfless generosity" of the Soviet
Union is being manifested by stripping these
countries of much of their production.
further implication was that these requisitioned
goods are being stockpiled for war purposes
rather than being devoted to raising the stand
ards of living even IN the captor country.


Significantly, neither the Czech nor the
Russian delegate made any direct reply to DR..
Lubin's inquiry and the Polish spokesman COM
planned only that his country's agriculture had
not kept pace with its gigantic" industrial
progress Soviet help, the Pole added, has been
"brotherly."


Whatever the precise facts are in this
particular situation behind the Iron Curtain, the
clear evidence of shortages in some OF the
satellite countries and the surprisingly open
admissions of such conditions encourage specu-
lation that unrest among the captive populations
may create a problem for the Kremlin masters
Traditionaly, the populations of Central Europe
have been fearful and antagonistic toward Rus
sian designs. There is little feeling that they
are willing allies today, and partnership main
tanned by force is bascally weak and unde-
pendable one.

divided between partieS-voted yesterday was
continuation Of the traditional Spois system for
the def1cit-plagued Post Office Department and
for customs officers and United States marshals.
The chief argument made on the floor against
the transfer of appointment power from the
President to the Post Office Department was that
this would place patronage in the hands of the
Postmaster General Overlooked, however, was

masters under the civil service competitive
system that prevails generally throughout the

chooses employees not because they have rem
dered some special service to the party in power

ton that they are qualified for appointment.


This would mean, of course, removing fat
bunch Of Federal plumS from the patronage
pie The Senate has dealt severe blow to the
determined efforts Of the Hoover Commission
and other supporters of the merit system to
eliminate the remaining vestiges of the once
popular system which gave to the victorious
party as much patronage gravy as possible
without regard to governmental efficiency.

CAPETOWN. South. africa, May
1.-Justice Minister J. r. Swart

position white and non-white
groups have threatened violence.

Daniel Malan have been pressed

for two days to explain why the
country has been combed for
police reinforcement during the
parliamentary debate on South
Africa's constitutional crisis.


Mr.. Swart would not disclose
precise reasons for the extra
precautions. But he limited
broadly the government expected
trouble over its new moves to
push through its white supremacy
program. He said the Nationalist
regime had noted these threats:


Leaders Of Negro, Indian and
mixed race groups have said they
intend soon to launch campaign
|of defiance against the race laws
which they deem unjust.


Leaders Of the militant Torch
Commando. group of white war
veterans bitterly opposing the Ma
tionalist government, have threat
ened to paralyze the country in a
day of national protest.


Opposition United Party leader

anti-government groups would
meet force with force" If the
Nationalist got rough.

Cape Argus suggested the govern
ment may be planning raids and
arrests of the Torch Commands
and the police have been brought
Ito Capetown to protect the gov
Iernment and Parliament against
possible counter demonstrations.


In the heavily-guarded Assem-
bly, yesterday, Mr.. Strauss formally
challenged the governments right
to push through its bill creating

Soviet builders also are far behind
schedule in construction of new
heavy and light cruisers. the
Merkur said.


There was no indication that
the submarine and topedo boat
program had failed in any respect
however.

BERLIN. June 2. - Scattered
clashes were reported today as
West Berliners sought to push
through Communist road blocks
sealing off the city from the sur
rounding Russian zone.


At one spot near the American
sector border a Communist
peoples policeman fired warning
shots to scare off West Berliners
who tried to enter the Russian
zone to get to their jobs.


Since Saturday, midnight, travel
from Allied West Berlin into the
Russian zone has been stopped
except for transit on the lifeline
roads to West Germany. Those
vital links were still open and
travel was reported normal.


Under their new regulations
the Communists require a special
police permit for travelling in East
Germany. Since nobody knows
where to get these, it means that
several thousand West Berliners
who work in the Russian zone will
be unable to get to their jobs when
the long Whitesuntide week end
ends tomorrow. A few anxious
people already tried it today.
When they were barred by Red
police Sentries at road blocks
arguments developed.


The east zone Communists claim
the security measures are neces-
sary as protection against alleged
Western spies and saboteurs. Com
munist newspapers and radios
have been attacking West Berlin
as a "viper's best of saboteurs and
Subversives.


West Berlin and Allied authori-
ties contend the measures are act
ually new attempts at harrassment
and strangulation of this city in
reprisal for West Germany hav-
ing signed political and military
alliances with the western world.

SEOUL, Korea, May 3l.-A
three pronged United Nations
tank k-infantry patrol smashed into
Communist lines today on the cen
trail front and the supporting foot
soldiers battled the Reds with
hand grenades.


A United States 9Th Army staff
officer said the Allied force struck
in the predawn darkness and
roamed Red-held territory west of
the Pukhan River for nine hours
before returning to its base.


The tank force was split into
three groups. One was assigned
to hit Red positions from the rear.
The second made a diversionary
attack and the third hit two OBJ
jectives. the main target of the
raid. The latter was covered by
artillery.

Communist defenders put up a
fight against the main force, but
Allied infantrymen drove them
from their positions with hand
grenades. Then the tank force
systematically destroyed Commu-
mist emplacements in the area.


The staff officer said at least ~
Reds were killed.


Patrol action across the rest of
the 155-mile front was reported
as generally light today.


The Air Force reported that
American Saber jet pilots shot
down two Communist jets over
Northwest Korea today.


The 5th Air Force announcement
said the Sabre jets were flying
protective cover for er-bomb-
ers hitting Red rail lines in ex-
treme northwest Korea.


No Allied Planes Lost.
The Air Force said no Allied
planes were lost in air combat last
week, a sharp reversal from the
week before when the Red jets
held a 5-4 advantage. The past
week six Russian-made MIG ISIS
were downed.


During the seven-day period
ended Friday midnight. the Air
Force said, three B-26 bombers
failed to return from night at
tacks and one Mosquito control
plane was shot down by Red guns
In addition to the six MIG kills
the Air Force claimed two dam
aged and an unidentified night
fighter probably destroyed.


Allied fighter -bombers during
the week reported six locomotives
and 675 supply vehicles destroyed
or damaged.


Supporting troops. the fighter
bombers destroyed 430 Red bunk
ers, blew up two ammunition
dumps and inflicted $40 casual
ties. the Air Force reported.

ABOARD THE S. S. UNITED
STATES May 14.-This sleek and
shiny new passenger liner heads
for the open Atlantic today to
stretch her sea-legs in two days
of builders trials.


The 52,000-ton ship, Americas
challenge to Britain's two sea
Queens. the Mary and Elizabeth.
will ease down the James River.
through Hampton Roads. across
Chesapeake Bay and point her bow
eastward.


It's the first taste of the sea
for the $72 million maritime pal
ace, whose builders eagerly await
tomorrow'S speed tests, confident
she will prove herself faster ship
than the much heavier Queen
Mary, present holder of the record
for the fastest Atlantic crossing.


Largest Built in United States.


The United States is the largest
commercial vessel built in an
American Shipyard.


AS the big ship passes historic
Fort Monroe at Old Point Comfort,
engineers of the Newport News
Shipbuilding & Drydock Co., her
builders. will begin testing her dis
tilling plant.


Of Cape Henry, the engineers
start the first steam rate tests.
The ships high-pressure steam
turbines can turn up more than
165, 900 horsepower.


Speed Trial Tomorrow.


Later today the ship will make
her economy trial, which will
measure fuel consumption.


Early tomorrow the United
States will begin her speed trials.
Spokesman for the ships builders
say the results Of the trials prob
ably will remain a secret.


The liner will return to New
port News Friday.


Aboard for the trials are l.
200 crewmen and technicians and
some 600 passengers. The pas
sengers include officials of the
shipyard, the United States
Maritime Administration and the
United States Lines, which will
accept delivery of the ship next
month.

The overwhelming election victory of the
pro-French government of the Saarland on Sun
day indicates clearly currently popular pref
erence for retaining the present political and
economic ties with France. It does not how
ever, remove the tiny and ndustrially rich border
state from its historic role of being trouble
some issue in French German relations. Chan
cellor Adenauer and other West German leaders
already have declared they do not recognize the
vote as true expression of the Saarlanders' will


Prior to World War I, the Saar was part
of the German Empire and its population today
is largely Germanic in language and cultural
heritage. It's coal and steel economy, however.
is linked closely with that OF Alsace and Lorraine
and France sought annexation of the Saarland
when it regained the two other provinces after
the first war. The compromise reached then
was to place the little state under adninistra-
ton of the League of Nations, where it remained
until plebiscite of 1885 restored it to Germany.
Under French military occupation from 1945 to
1947, the territory was given internal political
autonomy and status of economic union with
France in the later year. The degree of political
independence was increased in 1850 and the
economic union was formalized by convention
which placed the valuable Saar coal mines under
French management for so years.


The Saarland has been prosperous in these
postwar years through its economic association
with France. In addition, Frances Foreign
Minister Schuman has cultivated pro-French
sympathies by proposing that the Saarlanders
share the management responsibilities in coal
and STEEL and that the territory be European
lied" by making Saarbrucken the capital OF the
supranational coal and steel community The
election reflects the effect of these suggestions.


Meanwhile, in resurgent West Germany the
issue of bringing the Saar back to ''the father
land" has become an increasingly bitter one.
Negotiations between Bonn and Paris over the
territory's future broke down few weeks ago,
and open German electioneering against the pro-
French government in Saarbrucken preceded the
Sunday vote Charges that the Europeanization
plan is merely a screen for making the Saar
permanent French protectorate were broadcast.
The fact that parties favoring return OF the
area to Germany were barred from the ballot
prompted call for boycott of the voting, and
drew criticism of the United States and Britain
for not insisting on "free" elections. It is on this
point that the West German leaders are disputing
validity of the balloting although s3 per cent of
the eligible voters were recorded. OF this sur
prisingly large turnout, about IS per cent sup
ported the pro-Frenchl government.

fantrymen smashed over the top
of Triangle Hill on Korea's CEN
trail front today and fought a saw

northern slope. Two miles to the
east, more than 1000 Reds coun-
terattacked troops of the South
Korean I'd Division on Sniper
Ridge.


Associated Press Correspondent

Division infantrymen on Triangle
were pushing single-tile down a
Communist trench leading to
towering Papa-San Mountain. i'm

A front-line officer said they

against flercely resisting Chinese
Reds.


A hastily erected cable hoist

top of Triangle where other 7th

expected Chinese counterattack.


COunterattack in Dark.


The Reds lashed out at South

met their charge with withering
machine-gun fire from the caves
and bunkers of Pinpoint Hill. the
central peak in the hill mass.

|close-quarter fightiEs swirled

The South Koreans seized Pin
point earlier today with flame
throwers and hand grenades.


American officers with the South
Koreans said many of the dead
Chinese found on Pinpoint had
committed suicide.


White Horse Cleared.

the Reds with high explosives
from their last hold on blood
soaked White Horse Mountain.


Gen. Mark Clark's headquarters

sands of United States soldiers

ing shifted from White Horse in

Reds with bombs, rockets and
flaming gasoline.

swirling mantle of protection as
the attacking doughboys scram.
bled up the steep, sandy slopes o1

roared in support. But the foe
cut down the usually savage
Chinese mortar fire.

said the American casualties were
much lighter than yesterday. In
yesterdays opening battle, the
GIs reached the crest, only to be
hurled back by counterattacking
Chinese.

Once atop the crest today
American mortar crews lobbeo
smoke shells into the valley just
to the north. These cut down
visibility of Chinese artillery
spoilers on towering Papa-San
Mountain.
On White Horse Mountain
South Korean engineers tunneleo

tions. They planted stacks oi
land mines, then withdrew.


The mines exploded with deaf
ening roar and the whole noun.

1T just about blew the top of

Everybody's mad at the bootlegger,
but the bootlegger, squatting uncon-
cerned beside his still in the South
eastern hills. goes right on making
moonshnie and money. Some say
he's selling more than the legal dis
tillers.


Uncle Sam. who feels that whisky
is fair game for taxes. is mad because
the bootlegger doesn't pay any taxes
or buy any license.


The distiller, who is trying to make
an honest million, is mad because the
bootlegger cuts into the trade.


And the man on the street-at
least the man who likes little illegal
nip now and then-is mad because
the high cost Of living has touched
the trade in hootch.


Confusing Statements


All this anger vented on the boot
logger has brought about some con-
fusing statements. Men In the liquor
industry beat the drums for q cut IN
the excise tax. The high tax. they
say, makes q heyday for the boot
logger. They point with alarm to
statistics they have put together to
show that Federal, State and local
lawmen seized some 10000 illegal
stills last year. The law. they say.
has been swooping down on more and
more stills. This Is especially true,
the distillers add, since the United
States hiked the excise tax again last
November !.


The Internal Revenue Bureaus
Alcohol Tax Unit pooh -poohs such
talk. YEARLY, officials drag out their
own set of statistics to show that
they've been keeping the bootlegger
on the run at about the same rate
as before the new excise tax went
into effect.


The ATU's field men have seen no
great rush on the part Of the thirsty
men to replace his Old Shirtwaist
with white mule because Old Shirt
waist costs too much.


The ATU admits it's statistics don't
show what State and local officers
have seized. But 1t suspects there Is
lot Of duplication in the liquor
mems figures because the Federal
officers often take over a case from
the local people and then it is In
cluded on the Federal records.


Last May the tax men knocked on
S04 illegal stills. In May year ago
it was 896. And in 1910 the May
figure was 984.


1000 Stills Year


The number Of confiscated stills
has been settling down to yearly
average somewhat like that In the
prewar years-around 1000. In
1850 and 1851 the figure was about
10000, somewhat less than the whop-
ping numbers grabbed In prohibition
days.


In fiscal 1882, the Federal men
siezed 23,145 illegal stills. The fol-
lowing year-fiscal 1888, which got
under way July they got only
1892. That was the year Of repeal
and the figures cover six full months
Of repeal.


The number stayed pretty high fol-
the first few years after repeal. The
tax men say they were still knock
ing on the big boys" who prospered
during prohibition. Then it leveled
OF to the 1000 figure. Along came
the war. and sugar rationing, and
down went the bootleg business. II
slumped to about half what it had
been. Now It's back to the prevail
average.


The tax men say most Of today'i
bootlegging is confined to the South.
eastern part Of the United States. II

Growing demands for special session of

Unless there is a special session before the end

comply with constitutional requirement that
the State be redistricted two years after every
decennial census To leave the Assembly districts
as they are would be unfair to many areas which
have undergone substantial population growth
during the past decade.


The Assembly baked at the redistricting
task during its regular session earlier this year.
A comprehensive reapportionment plan was pre-
sented to the Legislature by special commits
sion but only the congressional redistrictng pro-
gram was adopted. Northern Virginia's new 10th
district was created after long and bitter fight
The commissions recommendations for legisla-
tive reapportionment would have given Northern
Virginia not only its own member of Congress but
one more State Senator and three more Delegates.
There are now only two State Senators and four
Delegates from all of the Arlington, Alexandria,
Fairfax-Fals ChurchPrnce William area. The

NEW YORK The Omega
Psi Phi Fraternity's annual boat
ride up the Hudson River this
year was so successful that it
almost caused a riot.

tickets for boat that could real
ly only accommodate 200. The size
of the crowd caused police to
send for reserves and three emer-
gency squads and nine radio pat
roll cars were rushed to the scene.


And though the crowd broke
through barriers, no nnishaps oc-
Cured, unless you want to count
the broken lunch baskets with
fried chicken and hard boiled
eggs cluttering the side walk
along with some ruined straw
hats and torn bits of clothing
Said Deputy Chief Inspector
William J. McQuade: "Only thu
intelligence and general good will
of the crowd kept this from turn
ing into something ugly"


The boat - Peter Stuyvesant'
- sailed only a half hour late
Packed to capacity, it left only
800 disappointed souls behind.

fence 512 feet high and 800 miles
long on the Soviet border.

reindeer from intermingling with
the Soviet variety. The valuable
herds have a tendency to cross
the border and get mixed up.


Finland and Norway, the Agri-

a treaty to get together once a
year and sort the animals out.

too well, because another stretch
Of fence is going up along the
Norwegian frontier.


Laplanders not only milk and
drive reindeer, they eat their flesh
and use their skins for clothing. :.

SEOUL, Oct. IA major drive
by $4,000 Chinese Communists,
which toppled seven allied hill po-
sitions in the first rush. was re-
newed in full fury tonight against
two key heights guarding the road
to Seoul


The Reds poured in heavy ar
tillery barrages against the hills,
then sent fresh troops charging
up the slopes which already were
Uttered with an estimated 1900
to 1900 Communist dead, front
reports said.


AS fighting ragged for the hills,
front-line officers called this big
gest Red assault in a year a "lim-
tied offensive. It so far had been
unable to dent the main allied
positions, but there was no letup.


At times it was melee of tanks,
artillery and mortar barrageS and
bayonetS as the Reds beat in
ceaSeleSs waves against the allied
lines across two-thirds of the 1885,
mile front.


Heights Command Seoul Road.


The hill positions that fell were
relatively minor allied outposts
stretching from one position near
the armistice town of Panmunjom
100 miles northeastward.


The main prize, however, was
White Horse Mountain and Ar
rowhead Ridge near Chorwon,
which is about As miles north of
Seoul. These heights command
the road to Seoul and here the
Reds threw their greatest punch.


Front reports said the attack
ing Chinese wore gas masks.
There was no explanation given.
The Reds repeatedly have accused
the allies of using gas in Korea
and possibly they had begun to
believe their own propaganda. The
allies insist they never have used
gas.


Associated Press Correspondent
Milo Farneti reported from the
front that a roaring artillery bar
rage powered today's assault. The
Reds pumped 200 rounds an hour
at each of the heights before the
infantry charge.


The first Red onslaught last
night gained the Reds some
ground at isolated points.


Red Losses Heavy.


Fighting was brutal. The Reds
threw men, tanks and artillery
into the battle, spread over two
thirds of the 155-mile battlefront.


But the Allies had known for
three days of the attack and were
ready for the assault.


The United States 9th Army
said the massive Red assault cap
tured seven hill positions. But
the Allied defenders stood their
ground at most places. The Army
added that many hundreds of
Reds were killed.


The Army said, "The Reds
main effort was thrown back
with heavy losses"


Allied warplanes roared over the
front today. hitting the Red lines.
Pilots said they destroyed two
Red tanks and about 80 bunkers.


One Allied outfit fought and
died to the last man in defending
a vital hill. The number of men.
presumably not large, was with
held.


Seeking Weak Point.


A front-line Allied officer indi-
Gated the Reds may have been
seeking a weak point where their
troops and tanks could pour
through to the south. Had they
succeeded, he said, they might
have cut off the entire Seoul area.
Wave, after wave of fanatical
Chinese began hitting the western
and central fronts last night. The
biggest force, nearly 5000 men,
ran straight into an allied trap
and was badly mauled.


The main Red blow hit White
Horse Mountain and Arrowhead
Ridge, near Chorwon. The Reds
opened the floodgates of a re-
servoir in an unsuccessful effort
to cut off allied reinforcements.
1t. William D. Lansford of Los
Angeles said the allies knew the
attack was imminent when the
Yokkok River, which circles both
hills, began to rise.


Floodgates Opened by Reds.


That meant the Reds had
opened the floodgates of Pongnae
Reservoir. But the allies had pre-
pared for that by fixing rock fords.
cable crossings and a helicopter
landing strip.


Allied officers knew three days
ago the attack was coming. They
did not say how they learned that.
They brought up fresh troops,
tanks and big guns.


When the Chinese attacked they
were met with a blistering bar
rage Of fire.


Between 800 and 900 Reds were
killed at White Horse alone. An
other $50 died at Arrowhead
Ridge.


Mr.. Farneti at the front said
the fighting produced the first
tank battle since the early days
Of the war. One RuSSian-built
T-34 tank was knocked out.

VERDEN, Germany, Oct. 27.-
Four thousand former members
of Hitler's dreaded SIS elite guard
cheered eX-Gen. Hermann Ramcke

lied soldiers of war crimes and
demanded the release of all $50

The SIS troopers assembled in

standarte," and members of the
elite regiments Deutschland" and
"Germania."


Fighting for FatherIand.


Ramcke, a paratroop general

man wartime leaders, told the SIS
men they had been fighting for
their fatherland as well as any
other German soldiers and that
therefore, "all defamation of their
honor must stop"


"All those Allied officers and
soldiers who bombed German
cities are also war criminals"
Ramcke said.


IF our soldiers are convicted
as war criminals then it was also
la war crime when the Allies
bombed unprotected German citiesV
and when the Allies now invent
atom bombs" he said.
These remarks were almost
drowned in cheering.


Some former SIS men answered
with calls of Eisenhower is a
schweinehund (pig dog)."
Rancho urged SIS troopers not
to take up arms again in any
cause as long as Germans were
still held in Allied prisons. He
claimed that 1880 German SOL
diers were involved in war crimes
and denazification trials after the
war. He asserted that they were
sentenced to a total of 4.166 years
in prison.


Ramcke himself was released
last year from a French war
crimes prison.


Explains Speech.


Former SIS Gen. Felix Steiner
summoned reporters after the
meeting and hastily told them
Ramcke was a guest speaker and
that he and the other SIS veter-
ans refused to identify themselves
with his allegations.


Earlier, Steiner had urged his
men at the rally to support plans
for united Europe.


"We SIS men never fought for
the Nazi party but rather for our
fatherland. Therefore, we are
not war criminals and not better
or worse than the millions Of
others who fought for their coun-
tries during the war;" he said.

NEW ORLEANS "Un Petit
Mardi Gras" "a little Mardi
Gras-takes place at the famous
Harmony Street wharf in New
Orleans every two weeks, when
one of the modern Delta pas
genger liners leaves New Orleans
for South America.


Almost every port in the world
has some kind Of ship departure
ceremony-the Aloha parties in
Hawaii. natives diving for coins
in some South Pacific ports.


With the numerous lines max
ing regular passenger trips to
Latin America Delta, United
Fruit, Alcoa and others-the docks
of New Orleans are gay spots, in
deed, during sailing time. A dis
tinctive Crescent City celebration
has been developed over the years
for ship sailings.


Passengers Line Rails


The Delta sailing parties, given
at the departure Of the Del Norte,
the Del Sud and the Del Mar. are
typical of these petits Mardi Gras.
After the passengers have ar
rived aboard the departing ship,
they line the rails to participate
in and witness the celebration.
Indeed, they are very much like
the maskers atop one of the deco
rated floats in a regular Mardi
Gras parade, because often they
throw gaily painted trinkets to
the crowd on the docks below.


Soon confetti and streamers
make their appearance. and these
brightly colored decorations add
to the gaiety of the occasion.
Gathered along the dock, in addi-
ton to the friends and relatives
of the passengers, are many on
lockers who enjoy entering into
the fun


To make the setting complete,
Papa CeleStin and his famous
Dixieland Jazz Band provide the
music and rhythm for this festive
gathering. Papa Celestin typif1es
gay old New Orleans, for he is
one of the original group of jazz
musicians. who made Dixieland
music famous along Basin street
and Bourbon street in old New
Orleans many years ago.


Party Carried Into Homes


All during the celebration. Delta
Line features an on-the-spot radio
broadcast so that many Orlean-
fans at home may take part in
the bon voyage party. Announcers
and interviewers wander through
the assembled crowd. talking to
onlookerS and passengers alike,
and occasionally picking up one
OF Papa Celestin's famous num-
bers.


Finally, "All ashore that's going
ashore" is heard. The gangplank
is pulled away, the liner heads
down the Mississippi for the
golden ports of the Spanish Main
and the strains of when the
Saints Go Marching In" from
Papa Celestin's band gradually
fade away.

SEOUL, Jan. 4.-Allied in
fantrymen stormed through heavy
mortar and small arms fire today
and recaptured priced Christmas
Hill on the east-central Korean
battle front.


Communist troops had attacked
and won the hill after dark. The
assault touched of see-saw fight
that lasted throughout most of
the night.


Changed Hands Repeatedly.


The peak had changed hands
repeatedly since Chinese troops
seized it on Christmas Day. The
hill is west of Mundung Valley.


Along the rest of the 145-mile
battle front. patrols of both sides
probed and fought minor skir-
miShes.


The weather was milder after
a week of bitter cold.


The slightly clearing skies
brought out Allied airmen in a
limited number of flights. The
5th Air Force flew 70 sorties
against Communist supply lines
and front positions yesterday and
last night.


Allied Squads Cut OFF.


The Christmas Hill assault
began at 7:35 pm. Thursday when
about 40 Communists attacked
and cut of the two Allied squads.


Allied troops counterattacked
after midnight against intense
mortar and small arms fire. The
Reds had built up their forces.
Communist troops drove back the
Allied force.


Just before dawn, the U. N.
command troops attacked again
and won the hill.

the first 20 days of August. United
Nations Sabre jet pilots shot down

only one Allied plane was downed

probably the most clean-cut VIC

The remnants of a South Caro-
lima hurricane which swept across
Maryland this week has done
some damage to the States crops,
Maryland's crops reporters said


Rains accompanied by high
winds downed corn and tobacco
crops in areas west of the Chesa-
peake Bay, the weekly survey of
crops conditions said.


Meanwhile, ground which had
been prepared for fall seeding was
washed considerably in the same
sections. Seed beds of lespedeza
hay were washed badly in Central
and Southern Maryland.


Cutting of tobacco continued
during the week, the survey re-
ported, unhampered by rains until
Monday when the crop was
Knocked down by rain and wind


The survey, issued jointly by the
University Of Maryland Extension
Service, the Federal Bureau OF
Agricultural Economics and the
Weather Bureau, said it was diff
cult to measure the effect of the
heavy rains on the tomato crop in
Central Maryland.


The harvest of tomatoes con-
tinued in all sections. but volume
moving to Gamers again was
lighter than normal. Cracked and
small-sized fruits have been very
common this season. the report
said.

riots at Bordeaux over food since

ported this morning that order

nights violent outbreak. Scream
ing inmates touched off the fresh
fires a few hours later.


Guards had been unable to con-
f1ne the prisoners in their cell
blocks because of the smashed
locks. The prisoners roamed the
main corridor and adjacent corri-
dors at will. Outside the walls,
yelling could be heard.

minor. Ten police squad cars
sped to join heavily-armed squads
who had been on guard since last
night. Police used tear gas bombs
and fired pistols over the rioters
heads.

and Planning Commission would dovetail per-

OF general regional interest is the proposed inter-

highway planning is well illustrated in the inter-
county freeway project. This major boulevard Is
needed to handle croSs-country traffic needs OF

larger purpose of bypassing through traffic

fiict The Maryland planners have agreed on
route that is in accord with the National Capital
Park and Planning Commissions master plan for
a belt road encrcling Washington outside the
Districts boundaries. The link would connect the
Georges County with the planned route of the
National pike through Montgomery County.
These widely separated approaches to Washing
ton from the North and West eventually would
cross the Potomac River on new bridges and
feed into Shirley Highway and U. S. Route l.

National Capital Park and Planning Commission
is under study by the Regional Highway Plan
ming Committee, which is preparing its own
recommendations, based on comprehensive traffic
checks. It should not prove difficult to reconcile
any differences which may develop between the

More rain is on the way to
water-logged Washington.


The Weather Bureau was not
predicting how much will fall

expected to arrive sometime to-
morrow night.


The rain, now drenching the
Southwest, moved across the
Mississippi into Western Illinois

forecaster said.


Potomac Still High.


The Potomac River, swollen by
heavy rains last week, remained
stationary today at feet over
floor stage above Key Bridge. The
water was expected to begin
receding this afternoon.


Tides below the bridge were
running about three feet above
normal today, the same as yester-
day. Most roads in the Washing
ton area which were closed by
high water have been reopened to
traffic.


Montgomery County Police at
Rockville said they expected
Whites Ferry over the Potomac
near Poolesville would get back in
operation sometime today.


All streams feeding the Potomac
and Rappahannock rivers were re-
ceding and barring another heavy
rain the rivers were expected to
get back to normal this week.


Rain Falls In South.

most of Texas, Missouri. Arkansas,
Oklahoma and Northern Louisi-
ana. The rain which soaked Wash
|ington last week moved over the
Great Lakes during the night and
was centered over the Eastern
Hudson Bay area this morning.


The Washington area was to
have clear skies today with high
temperature of around 81. Clouds
will move in tonight. 1t will be
cloudy and cool tomorrow.

rapid recovery to, Virginia from
SHOWS in the southwest section of

in the Friday night snowfall which
measured up to IL inches in some
areas. The Safe Highway Depart

The Friday after Thanksgiving is day that
attracts many shoppers to the stores in the down.
town area. The schools are closed and many
mothers evidently choose the opportunity to
take the youngsters on a Christmas preview
Other circumstances add to the crowd. This has
been demonstrated in the past.


But Washington seems to have been caught
by surprise last Friday-or else the number of
automobiles has increased to point that comes
very close to traffic saturation and traffic
paralysis. Tall tales are going the rounds of
the time spent on Friday by automobile drivers
trying to penetrate the shopping district from
as short distance away as Massachusetts, ave-
nue.. Parking lots and garages were jammed.
Delivery trucks, with supplies for such places
as restaurants, were completing their delayed
errands late in the day and even postponing
some of them until Saturday morning. Harassed
traffic policemen, with the sole idea of keeping
the intersections relatively clear, were sending
distressed motorists away from their intended
destinations. If Friday did not write new
record in downtown traffic congestion, it must
have come very near doing so.


One hopes that this condition was not
mere forestaste of traffic conditions that will
prevail when the real Christmas shopping rush
gets underway. But smart shoppers will do their
shopping early. And those who park their cars
out of the congested area and use public trans
portation will be wise. For there were times,
on Friday, when nobody was moving anywhere.

campaign to oust the governor.

hunting. The 5th Air Force said
pilots destroyed 20 Red supply

east coast but generally air strikes

position northeast of Kumhwa on
the central front. They were
thrown back after the skirmish
closed to within hand grenade
range.


Red Position Seized.
Two Allied patrols on the cen
tral front occupied a Communist
position southeast of Kumsong
after daylong battle yesterday


Communist patrols probed on
the central front but there were
no reports Of positions changing
hand.


In Tokyo, Gen. Matthew B.
Ridgway's headquarters said the
Reds have built a defense belt
a crude "Siegfried Line"-across
Korea since truce talks began nine
and a half months ago.
An official Army analysis said
the Red buildup does not yet pose
a threat to U. N. forces. The re-
port placed Communist troop
strength at more than 10000
men, mostly Chinese, and said
more than half the Red air force
lof $500 planes was jet-powered.
Allies Still Control Air.
Allied warplanes still control the
air over Korea. the report con-
tinued, but this has not prevented
the Communists from building ur
their front line supplies. It added
that the enemy has shown the
ability Ito move armies into and
out Of the line without suffering
casualties"


Red troop changes and other
buildups have not ''in themselves
indicated offensive intentions,
the report declared. but the Reds
have shown their intention oi
maintaining a strong position il
Korea"

VANCOUVER, B. c., Dec. 90
The Canadian freighter Maplecove
limped toward Vancouver today,
using her damaged rudder like a
splintered crutch.


After temporary repairs to her
steering gear in mid-Pacific, the
10,000-ton merchantmen strained
portward at 10 knots, trying to
bring her 81 crew members home
in time for Christmas.


The Maplecove and the rescue
tug Island Sovereign, dispatched
from Vancouver Thursday night,
were closing at a combined speed
of % knots.


With a break from the weather,
the two will meet Sunday morning
about 500 miles off the British
Columbia coast. If the Maple
cove can keep under way, the Is
land Sovereign will provide only
escort.


The Maplecove, bound from
Yokohama to Vancouver, broke
down Thursday 1850 miles west
of here. She shrugged off an
angry gale and made repairs
which enabled her to resume
travel.

from the Army and will report to
the Daytona Beach training camp
in March.

years ago, Camp was considered

lands farm system. Hurting for

text:
THE TROUBLE WITH American


i air power, according to recent
report of Lyndon Johnson's Senate
Preparedness subcommittee, is that
too much attention has been paid
to "gimmickry and gadgetry," and
not enough to the serious business
OF making planes.


Last week the Nations latest
airborne gimmick, equipped with
various gadgets including one
called television, rose from the
fight deck Of the Navy's 27,000- ton
carrier Boxer and headed for North
Korea. It was an obsolete Grum-
man Hellcat dive bomber, with
1-ton bomb fastened to its belly.
No pilot sat at the controls. The
take-off was directed from the car
rier. AS ! the Hellcat gained alti-
tude, its custody was assumed by
the crew of a mother plane,"
Douglas tAD-2) Skyraider, hovering
nearby.


The two planes disappeared to
the northwest and soon crossed the
Korean coastline. They did not
have to stay together: BY tele-
vision, the technicians in the
mother plane saw what the pilot
would have seen from the Hellcat,
and transmitted their electronic
orders accordingly. AS the drone
approached the target area, a
valley heavily protected by anti
aircraft guns, it was put into .
dive.


BuIIseye


On the television screen in the
mother plane, miles away, the
target loomed larger with each
passing second. Then the screen
suddenly went blank. The Hellcat
and its blockbuster warhead, un-
erringly guided to their rendezvous
with death, had scored a direct hit.


The robot, of course, was de-
stroyed with it's target, but there
were more where it came from. In
other strikes from the Boxer last
week, pilotless kamikazes performed
such feats of accuracy as knocking
the center support from under a
key Communist bridge $50 miles
away, and blocking the mouth of
a railway tunnel. In the latter
instance, the televiSion screen re-
corded the doom of two North
Korean railway workers who, fear
ing they were about to be strafed,
frantically pumped their handcar
into the tunnel just ahead Of the
diving plane.

nual Shell Fair. February Is, 16

teur shell collectors from various

shelling on the snow-white sands

waters of this area cannot be
oVeremphasized and will bring

nature and will create a complete
feeling of serenity. A shell COL
lection made here will bring you
pleasure throughout the years.


individuals who take time to

SEOUL. Korea. May 14.-Small

Allied patrol killed SO Communist
troops in an early-morning raid.
The patrol drove the Reds out of
an advanced position on the
central front and held it for As
minutes until the Communists
counterattacked.


The longest pre-dawn skirmish.
also on the central front, broke
out when Reds probed in the
Kumhwa sector where United
Nations tank patrols tested Chi
nese defenses Monday and Tues
day. The Skirmish was between
two Red squads and Allied out
posts. The Communists finally
pulled out at 4:45 am. Nearby,
two Communist platoons fought
nearly an hour and a half with
Allied outposts. Thirty-one at
tackers were reported killed in the
two fights.


Lighter probes and long range
rifle duelS erupted elsewhere.
Air Force and naval planes
reported nearly 200 new cuts were
blasted in North Korea's patch
work rail lines Tuesday. The Air
Force reported its raiding planes
destroyed IS Red buildings and
damaged 25. Five enemy planes
were also shot down.


Biggest blcwoff was the work of
the guns of the United States
destroyer Lowry. It's shells touched
off fireworks display in a Com
munist ammunition dump at be-
seiged WonSan on the east coast.
Farther north a whaleboat from
the minesweeper Symbol, manned
by eight American seamen, res
cued North Korean civilian from
under the eyes of Red troops. The
Communist soldiers watched the
operation but didn't fire shot.

Simplicity marked the garden
party yesterday of the British
Ambassador and Lady Franks who
celebrated the birthday anniver-
sary of their new sovereign, Queen
Elizabeth II. The weather was
perfect and the beautiful Sloping
lawn velvety green. Everywhere
the luxuriance of early summer
in Washington was evident. The
crimson climbing roses over the
low walls about the garden; the
more formal rose garden close to
the house; and the trees and
scrubs edging the lawn were at
their best.


The Ambassador and Lady
Franks stood in front of a clump
of tall lockwood at the foot of the
steps from the terrace to greet
their several hundred guests.
Members Of the embassy staff
escorted guests down the steps and
presented them to the hosts. Lady
Franks wore a very becoming short
frock Of white with small dark
brown figure, the skirt full and
the bodice having square neck
line and made long over the shoul-
ders in place of sleeves. The two
younger members Of the family,
Caroline and Alison, were here.
there and everywhere, wearing
deep rose color dresses made alike.
They, too were very friendly and
remembered more than one guest
from the party last year, an ac-
complishment for one just enter
ing her teens and one several years
younger.


England TronspIonted


The scene yesterday as one
stepped out onto the terrace and
looked down onto the lawn was
typically English as were the
luscious Strawberries and whipped
cream served to follow the custom
at home. Neither the berries nor
the cream came from Devon
shire but were nonetheless de-
licious. Three long buffet tables
were set up on the outer edges of
the lawn. Each table was centered
with a birthday cake which had
sprays of roses in the icing and a
cluster of the natural bright bios
SONS in a bowl.


The delicious cold coffee with
ice cream was very welcome and
there also was a bar where Scotch
and soda as well as other drinks
were to be had.

panied by Mr.. Roy Leif1en, was
among those calling to wish the
new Queen many happy returns
of the day." She wore a becom-
ing dark-blue eyelet-embroidery
dress with a wide band Of pale
green tulle about her head and
tied in large bow at the left
side. She spent some time among
the guests on the lower lawn but
grew camera shy" when asked
to pose with Mrs. Estes Kefauver.
The latter wore black organdy
with a wide -brimmed black hat
the crown and top of the brirn
covered with white lace.


The Australian Ambassador and
Mrs. Percy Spender were congrat-
ulated on all sides for his birth
day award from the Queen. How
ever, he will not be Sir Percy
until he goes to England and re-
ceives the honor personally from
the Queen.


Secretary of State and Mrs.

Near Soviet Boundary.

northeastern tip of Hokkaido when

ing from the direction of the Ku-
rile Islands. It's path merged with
that of the B-29 image, the Air

before disappearing off the radar
screen.

were over japanese territory when
they dropped out of sight.

JAKARTA, Indonesia, Oct 20.
-Indonesia's capital returned to
near normal today after a week
end Of explosive political tension.


Tanks and artillery were with
drawn from strategic positions
throughout the city yesterday.
Army roadblockS were removed
and two hours were chopped off
the emergency curfew.


But the political crisis which
touched off mob scenes Friday re-
manned unsettled. Parliament's
chairman announced the legis-
lators would continue indefinitely
a recess called after the dramatic
session Thursday in which they
adopted a motion censuring the
Defense Ministry. The mobs had
demanded that the Parliament re-
sign.


Still hanging is the parlia-
mentary motion, which demands
reorganization of the Defense
Ministry and of the, Army high
command. The 7-month-old cab
met of Premier Wilopo was ex-
pected to fall over the issue but
announced it would remain in Of
flee, at least temporarily.

facilities during the first month.

LONDON. Dec. 18. - Heavy
SHOWS in the wake of battering
gales covered most of central and
northern Europe today with
Yule-like white blanket but mod
Grating winds allowed two big
transatlantic liners to get under
way for New York-hours late.


Snow was reported from Italy,
Switzerland, Belgium, Germany
and the Scandinavian countries.
In France, however, there were
threats of floods around the Bor-
deaux area due to melting SHOWS


The 53,329-tor liner United
States finally pulled out of her
berth at Southampton. England,
more than 20 hours after sched-
uled sailing time, and the French
liner Liberte also left LIE Havre.
France, 10 hours late. Both had
been delayed by English Channel
gales. with winds registering up
to 80 miles an hour.


The United States, which holds
the Atlantic speed record, suffered
minor damage to her bridge and
observation deck yesterday when
high winds slammed the vessel
against the dockside as she was
being maneuvered away from her
moorings in a vain attempt to get
out of port.


The drop in the winds also
permitted removal of 20 officers
and men from the Swedish mine
sweeper Orskar, aground off the
southeast coast of Sweden, near
the port of Kalmar. Thirty other
officers and men remained aboard
the vessel and Swedish navy ex-
perts said they expected to have
the 330-ton ship af1oat in a few
days.


Gale warnings were broadcast
for the Baltic last night, but
there was no mention of them in
weather reports today.

British soldiers stationed nearby

lean 121st Evacuation Hospital.

crossed the bridge and remained
upright. But two Of the three

Witnesses said some passengers
were thrown into the stream, 40

when we heard the explosion

I STOCKHOLM, Sweden, July 81.
Six Swedish Communists were
convicted of selling vital defense
secrets to Russia today and two
were sentenced to life imprison-
ment at hard labor. A seventh
was acquitted.
The Swedish government
charged them with turning over
to the Russians full details of
their country's northern defenses
against any Russian attack across
neighboring Finland.


Fritiof Enbom, 33-year-old con-
tessed master mind of the Soviet
spy ring. and his chief accom-
Iplice. Jugo Gjersvold, both drew
life terms at hard labor. The
lringleader's younger brother, Mar
tin Enbom, drew a seven-year SEN
ltence.


Councilman Convicted.
Others convicted and sentenced
were:


Arthur KarlSson, 42, a Com
munist member of the town coun-
Gil of Halmsted in South Sweden
karlsson. who arranged the elder
Enbom's contact with Soviet En-
bassy officials. received one year
and eight months imprisonment.


Fingal LARSON, 40, a railway
worker. whom the government ac-
cused OF sending regular reports
to Enbom on railway security
measures. He drew five years at
hard labor.


Lillian Ceder, 81, Fritiof Enbom's
girl friend, whom police charged
operated a short-wave transmitter
Enbom received from the Rus
slams. She was given eight months
but the court ruled the three
months she has spent in custody
since her arrest would count in
this period.


Clerk Wins Acquittal.
The seventh accused member of
the ring, acquitted for lack of
proof, was Tage Wickstrom, 81, a
clerk in the army fortification con-
struction bureau.


The Enbom brothers and Giers-
void confessed. The elder Enbom,
an editor and agitator. said he
had collected military and in
dustrial information for the Rus
slams for six years, turning it
over to Soviet Embassy officials in
return for cash.
He admitted giving the Soviets
data on Sweden's strongest mod
ern fortress, near Boden, IS miles
from the Finnish border. Other
information collected included
maps Of secret military roads
forts and field Notifications,
locations Of transformer stations,
ammunition and fuel dumps and
up-to-date lists Of ornaments and
military equipment. 49,.
Russia. Rejects Protest.


The Swedish Foreign Office
sent a sharp protest last month
to Russia charging that officials
of the Soviet embassy in Stock
holm had worked with Swedish
citizens in spying against this
country. The note bluntly told
the Soviets to stop espionage
activities in Sweden. Russia re-
jected the note declaring that its
embassy here had no connection
with the Swedish spy ring. She
added that the charges were in
lventions aimed at deteriorating
friendly relations between Russia
and Sweden.


The protest coincided with an
other sharp exchange of notes
in which Sweden accused Rus
sian jet fighters Of shooting down
two unarmed Swedish planes
within two weeks over interna-
tional waters of the Baltic. Rus
sia rejected that protest as we'll,

eign plane caught straying over

The cotton textile industry ap-

corner toward better business.


The lights were burning late for
second and in some cases third
shifts in many of the textile
centers.


Buying came back to New York's

remained firm.

year.

the highest since March 8.


Steel production pushed close to
the two million-ton mark as ad-
ditional facilities returned to full
operation and the plants ran at
05.4 per cent of rated capacity.


Retail stores reported little
better business than a year ago

week. The Federal Reserve Bank

up bit nationally, although some

q year ago.

decline in milk production and a

VIENNA. Austria, Nov. 24.-An
Austrian Communist newspaper
admitted today that the Reds ar
rested the missing American Field
brothers. Noel and Herman. who
disappeared behind the Iron Cur
tain three years ago.


Since Noel Field. former State
department employe, vanished in
Prague in May. 1949. and his
brother Herman, a Cleveland
'Ohio) architect, disappeared in
Warsaw in August. 1949, one thing
has never been clear:


Were they kidnapped, along with
Noels German-born wife, Herta,
and his adopted daughter. or dio
they flee the West of their own
free will?


Referred to As Spies.


The Communists in their vari-
Gus show trials including the
present accusation of Rudolf

worked for the wartime United
States Office of Strategic Services

West. however, there have been
many suggestions that the broth
erS were double agents and that

VolkSstimme today disclosed then
arrest. 1t was wrong. said the

rest. the American State Depart
ment voluntarily said they had a

ly has sought information from

checking out of a Prague hotel,
ostensibly to go to Budapest. Her
mann Field boarded a plane for
Prague in Warsaw but never ar
rived. Noel's wife. Herta, vanished
at the Prague airport while await
ing for her brother-in-law's ar
rival.


Noel's adopted daughter, Mrs.
Robert Wallach. vanished among
the ruins of Berlin in 1850 after
arriving from Paris. presumably
on hunt for her foster parents.

BERLIN, May 30.-Fifteen
thousand Communists. surging in
from the Russian zone for an
anti Western demonstration,
touched off a savage clash with
West Berlin police last night in q
growing war of nerves.


Club-swinging police injured
hundreds of the invaders. arrested
800 and broke up the demonstra-
ton after an hour of milling in
the downtown borough Of Kreuz-
berg. in the American sector.


Tear gas squads were ready. but
were never needed. There was no
gunfire.


Rowdies Dispersed.


The riot was set off by a group
Of thousand brawny Commu-
niSts distributing leaflets denounc-
ing West Germany's newly signed
peace contract with the Allies and
calling for German unity, Soviet
style.


After a series of short but sharp
brawls with highly trained West
Berlin police platoons. the rowdies
were showed into side streets and
dispersed. Most of the other
demonstrators, teen-age youths
kept out of the fight.


Reports that $4,000 strongarm
men had been ordered into other
areas in the United States, British
and French sectors kept police on
the alert, but proved unfounded.


Bonn Denounces Rumors.


The rioting was timed with a
visit of British Foreign Secretary
Eden, who told West Berlins
Parliament and people to stand
firm. He declared the Red pres
sures were passing phases" and
forecast eventual German unity
in peace, with this city as the
capital.


In the West German capital Of
Bonn, Chancellor Konrad Aden-
auer's government stamped hard
on rumors that West Berlin and
its % million people would be
given up to the Russians without
a fight. Declaring the rumors
were circulated for political pur-
poses to cause unrest" the gov
said they are totally
without foundation.

FRANKFURT, Germany, Sept.
15.-The United States Army has
taken accreditation cards away
from three members Of the Soviet
military liaison mission here and
ordered them out of the American
zone. The action retaliated for
similar Russian measures last
month against three American
military men in Potsdam.


United States Army headquar-
tiers announced yesterday 1t had
forced the three Russians a
lieutenant colonel, a captain and
Ia private-to give up their passes
ION September S. Since then they
have remained in their mission
compound here.


Charges Called Unfounded.
Three American Army men Of
the same ranks were arrested by
the Russians north of Berlin in
August and charged with spying
on q restricted area. The Soviets
later released the three but de-
manded their withdrawal from
the United States mission at Pots
dam, in the Soviet zone.


The United States Army an
nounced yesterday that its care
full investigation" has proved the
espionage allegation unfounded.
It did not disclose whether the
three men had been recalled, as
the Russians demanded.


Action I'm Retaliation.


To retaliate, American Army
officials said they notified the
colonel who heads the 11-man
Russian mission here on Au-
gust 28 that he must surrender
the passes Of three Of his staff.
When the order was ignored,
United States military police on
September 5 took stations at the
entrance to the mission with
orders to stop any Soviet military
personnel from leaving. Shortly
after the passes were surrendered
and the police detail was re-
moved.


The Russians charged the
Americans with blockading their
Frankfurt mission, threatening
its members and forcing them to
hand over certain documents.

OMAHA. Nebr., April 18.-The
Missouri River threw its worst al
Omaha and Council Bluffs today
with an army of workers still win
ming the battle to hold the great
river in its Strait-jacket of bikes


River forecasts said the Mis-
souri, is at cresting stage and will
continue to crest all day.


At $50 am. the level was 1924
feet, compared with the flood
stage of 10. Some minor rising
and falling will occur before the
level begins to drop some "a hours
hence, the Weather Bureau said.


The predicted high had been
Bis feet. But at this near-phe-
nomenal level even the action of
the wind can raise or lower the
gauge readings by foot or more.


The critical hours began before
dawn when the slow-moving flood
crest began surging into the
7-mile-long funnel of sodden dikes
protecting the lowlands of the
twin cities of Omaha and Council
Bluffs, Iowa.


Next 48 Hours Critical.


The next 48 hours may deter
mine whether the tremendous
water pressures will burst through
levees and cause more suffering
and damage.


All night long soldiers and CT
william workers-more than $4,000
of them-toiled under foodlights
on the bikes here and on leveeS
downstream, where the rising
waters are expected to smash
through almost every farm dixie
all the way to Kansas City.


Doctors, lawyers, business ex-
ecutives. students. newspapermen
and other volunteers took their
turn heaving sandbags on the
bikes to strengthen them against
the most awesome floods the Mis-
souri, Valley has ever known.


The great battle was to get the
crest of the river safely past the
narrow Omaha channel, through
which the water is flowing at the
fantastic rate of 286 billion GAL
Ions per day.


North of Omaha, the Missouri
sprawls across the farm land for
as much as Is miles. Little
towns are inundated and farm
buildings stand with only their
roofs showing in the vast and
lonely wilderness from which all
living things have fled.


Channel Only 1000 Feet Wide.


For so miles upstream, the river
averages 10 miles in width-or
$4,000 feet. But in the narrowest
part of the Omaha Council Bluffs
channel the funnel is only 1900
feet wide. And the tide must be
passed through this slender bot
tleneck before the danger is past.


The river crest is monStrous,
creeping thing that moves slowly
with tremendous power. It strained
against the bikes here with a
pressure of more than 1850
pounds per square foot.


Through the night workers
rushed sandbags to weak points.
The water crept to the top of the
levees at some points and then
splashed against the splashboards
built to hold back the top few
inches of the rivers crest.


About 300 workers were con-
centrated during the night at a
danger point in the levee guard
ing the Municipal Airport on the
Omaha side of the river.


The airport-which was under
Z feet of water in the 1943 flood
is not in use and commercial
flights are operating from the
field at Offutt Air Force Base.


Form Human Chain.


The workers formed a 700-foot
human chain from the edge of the
northeastern runway, passing
sandbags across the sodden low
lands to build a secondary levee
This dixie was being built around
10-acre area into which water
was seeping from the main dixie.


Water oozed through Soggy
levees and through spongy earth
beneath them as danger signals
Levee patrols sent workers into
these points as quickly as they
were spotted.


The nerve centers in the fight
were command posts set up by
the Army Engineers under the
immediate direction of Brig.

rail traffic from West Germany

or fearing warlike developments
streamed across the border in
flight to West Germany.


Soldiers Brace Patrols.

East German Communist police
as border sentries. machine pistols
were issued to German policemen
and the number of fugitives dim
inished.


The three Western Allied COM
mandants in Berlin - British,
American and French-held a
special meeting today to discuss
the troubled situation. There was
no immediate indication whether
any new Allied action was con-
templated.

appealed to the Allies for a pre-
else definition Of the Western
powers security guarantee of Ber-
lin as a deterrent to further Rus
sian harassments.

The hepaticas are dainty little
early spring boomers that are
much desired for the shady gar
den. However, they must have a
soil rich in humus and not too
acid. The sharp-leaf hepatica of
the Alleghenies, needs soil less
acid than its neighbor. The he
paticas. because of the shape of
the leaves-3-lobed and rather
roundNtake another common
name from the color at time of
Towering. The blooms appear
above the old liver-colored foliage,
hence are sometimes called liver
leaf.


The hepaticas are dainty little
flowers and need a proper setting
as well as soil condition for most
effective growth and showing.
However, they transplant very
easily and should be in every wild
flower garden. Wildlings are pre-
ferred to cultivated plants be-
cause of the likelihood of rust and
other diseases.

acurate." He described the Allied

bers felt the increase should wait

greSs acts.

sioner, said failure to get the s.
cent tax would delay several prior
ity projects in the new road-build-

street bridge. the New York and

parkway, and the Southwest Free

tainly very keenly disappointed

to spend their money for improve
ments they have demanded"

money. the general said.

another reason for home rule"

now is devising a way to provide
the extra funds-possibly a bor-
rowing program.


"We're in bad fix as it is, even
with the tax increase" Gen. Rob-
inson said. "And without it, the
situation is hopeless"

mittee consideration of the pactS had not been

office, and to the fact that the French have not
yet ratified the pacts.

taken the position consistently, however, that
neither the committees nor the courts can change
the form of the agreements, that the under
standings were reached in honorable and honest
negotiations, and that the government is pledged
to seek their prompt ratification. Spokesman for
the government forces are now predicting that
the ratification will be obtained by approximately
the same vote as that most recently recorded.
While the discipline displayed in the 2207160 vote
tends to support this confidence, opposition led
by the Social Democratic Party bloc of 1870 is

April 5.-Armed police stood by

Under the wide powers it as
sumed in 1850, the nationalist gov
eminent can jail those who organ

Main significance. they say. lies

Council have come together virtu-
ally for the first time to fight for
their political goals: freedom to
organize politically and vote, free
dom to work and live where they
wish, improved housing, better
hospitals and more schools.


Messages Give Encouragement.

step-by step advance in their

taxpayer already is Smelling out

welfare, government spokesman

ally opposed to the Unions race
policies, have sent the non-whites
messages of encouragement on the
eve of their campaign. These in
clude the governments Of Iran, the
Philippines, Red China, midas
united provinces and Kashmir.

MANILA. Feb. 20.-The Philip
pines government today Cancelled
its policy of seeking new markets
for sugar and banned exports to
all countries except the United
States.


The decision was reached at a
conference between President
Elpidio Quirino and representa-
tives Of the sugar industry.


It was agreed also that surplus
sugar above the export quota for
the United States would be used
domestically to lower prices.


The new order followed months
of wrangling between the Quirino
administration, which favored
new markets. and sugar interests,
which opposed shipping sugar
elsewhere before filling the United
States quota.


Under the 1916 Trade Act. the
Philippines reserved an annual
quota of $4,000 tons for the
United States. This has not been
met because Of crop failures and
wartime damage to installations.

NEW DELHI-The shooting war
going on in the desert wilderness
Of Western India might raise the
envy Of any Hollywood movie writ
er.


It's the governments campaign
against India's Dacoits-blood-
thirsty, hard-riding bandits who
for decades have infested the
former princely states Of Jodhpur
Jaipur and Bikaner.


The war goes on before a back
drop Of camel-riding gangsters,
night raids and murders, kidnapped
women, and straight-shooting po-
lcemen.


Twice recently Prime Minister
Nehru commended police heroes in
the struggle, determined men who
followed their quarry for days and
finally brought them in dead.


Bandit Leader Killed.


The last commendation came
after police trapped and killed
bandit leader Pabudan Singh and
five Of his gang after a six-hour
gun battle. The police fired more
than TOO bullets into the bandit
hideout, and faced more than 400
shots in reply before all six Da-
colts died.


The anti-crime war drove India'S
most famous Dacoit across the
border and into a Pakistan prison
cell. He is Bhupat. sometimes
called the Robin Hood of Saurash-
ira state. India placed reward
equal to $4,000 on his head and
jailed several minor princes for
assisting him and his gang.


When he fled into Pakistan-
where he was arrested for carry
ing unlicensed firearms and jailed
for year-Bhupat faced IS mur-
der charges. Most of them re-
suited from raids on rich villagers
Of Saurashtra state.


In Parliament Nehru told how
Q special police inspector trailed
Bhupat night and day. riding on
horseback continuously for more
than a week, until Bhupat evaded
arrest by slipping into Pakistan.


Modern police methods play a
minor part in the desert warfare.
Pursued and pursers alike ride
camels or horses. Motor vehicles
find it hard going in the deserts.
Occasionally airplanes help locate
fleeing gangs.


Fear And Hero Worship.


Both fear and hero worship play

such bandits as the now dead
Pabudan Singh. For more than
16 years he led band Of outlaws
through the Rajasthan deserts,
hiding with friendly villagers
whenever police pursuit became
too close.

princely standing have helped the
DacoitS. Government officials say

Six on British Squad.

the Surrey tournament last week
at Surbiton. England, and with
Miss Brough is playing this week
at Manchester.

four who is not in top condition.

doctor told her 1t was nothing

United States carriers. staging the
greatest Navy air strike of the
Korean war, struck within sight
and sound Of Soviet Siberia today
in the United Nations air cam
Ipaign of utter destruction for Red
military installations.


The attack by 164 Navy
bombers and fighters from the
Boxer, Essex and Princeton hit an
Oil refinery and an iron works in
extreme Northeast Korea. Pilots
reported the Reds were SO totally
surprised they didn't even throw
up fax.


The refinery was at Aoji, IL
miles south of the Siberian border
and northernmost air target Of
the war. The iron mine works
was at Musan, across the Tumen
River from Manchuria.


The Navy said 70 per cent Of
the Musan works-including ore
concentrating and hydrogen plants
was destroyed and the synthetic
oil refinery at Aoji was left burn
ing with smoke rising 4 miles.

son home.

shortly afterward. Grover Wood
son and his family left the home
in fear.

found the shotgun and shot him
self.

office, which resulted in the custer

Board members.

not based on any public hearing.

eral rent controls since June Is.
1850. when they were abolished

Assembly. Rent controls had been
in effect there during World
War II.

The County Board Saturday
passed two resolutions. One.
under provisions of Public Law
96 passed by Congress last year,

controls until September 30.

next April 80, under new
law passed by the 1852 Con-
gress allowing communities and
counties to extend Federal rent
control if they request it.

declare the resolutions illegal and
to restrain Mr.. Henderson from
carrying them out.

The United States made clear
today that it will not lend Iran
money to make up the loss of oil
revenues resulting from Trans
dispute with Great Britain.


Iranian Premier Mossadegh
asked for a $120 million credit
when he visited Washington last
fall.


The State Department said to-
day this Government has told

the type requested at a time when
Iran has the opportunity Of re-
ceiving adequate revenues from its
oil industry without prejudice to
its national aspirations"


Iran nationalized her oil indus
