of the Anglo -Iranian Oil Co.
which had been operating the big
industry.


Mediation Unsuccessful.


The United States attempted to
mediate the Iranian-British dis
pute without success.


A World Bank mission has been
in Iran recently striving to work
out some basis for resuming oil
production, but the Mossadegh
government so far has turned
down it's proposals which report
edly involved the use Of British
technicians.


Premier Mossadegh was quoted

this week as saying the United
States had refused him financial
aid because he would not accept
British proposals for settling the
oil dispute.


The State Department denied
this today. asserting that the
United States has not made
Iranian acceptance of "any par
ticular proposals" a condition for
financial aid.


Settlement Is Possible. ,

ever:

sistently maintained that a settle
ment is possible in which the
legitimate interests of both Iran
and the United Kingdom will be
protected and which will make the
resumption of the oil industry
operation feasible and practicable
from the economic viewpoint"

said, applied only to the Iranians'
plea for help in meeting its bud
getary problems growing out OF its
loss of oil revenues. A separate
long-pending Iranian application
for a $25 million Export-1mport
Bank. loan to finance irrigation
and other agricultural develop
ment projects still is under con-
sideration.

ain summoned him back with

ade which effectively kept Iran

NEW YORK. Nov. 29.-Good
business. high production and still
more optimistic forecasts gave this
Nations economy healthy bloom
this week.


The Thanksgiving holiday cut
into the weeks output. But the
daily rate of production remained
at record or near record levels.


Many plants closed through the
week end. Employers were little
reluctant to take this step but
they said worker absenteeism is
usually heavy after a Thursday
holiday.


Auto Output Slows.


For instance, the auto industry
was slowed down sharply by the
holiday and many automobile
factories closed through Friday
and Saturday. Total assemblies in
United States and Canadian
plants dropped to 117.700 cars and
trucks from 1924 in the pre-
ceding week.


Industry circles in Detroit said
unless more materials and man
power troubles intervene, this
years output appears certain to
hit 4,350,000 units, the total al
lowed by the national authority.


Good news was pretty common
commodity this week. There was
a little disappointment over retail
sales, which haven't quite meas
ured up to expectations. For the
week ended Wednesday total dol
lar volume was estimated un-
changed to 4 per cent above a
year ago.


Merchants Hopeful.


Trade sources attributed some of
the disappointment to unseason-
able weather and some to an ap-
parent belief that many consumers
anticipate a little give in prices.


Most merchants, however, were
reported still holding the belief
that Christmas sales will establish
record highs. Gains in personal
income helped sustain their hopes.


Unemployment was lower than
at any time in the past seven
years, according to the Guaranty
Trust Co. of New York. In some
industries it was tough getting
additional help.

LYNMOUTH, Eng, Aug. 18.-I
Army engineers blasted and bull
dozed their way today through the
debris of flash food believed to
have drowned 80 persons in Eng
lands southwest resort coast.


Thus far nine bodies have been
recovered from among the rain
washed boulders and house wreck
age along a 15-mile stretch of the
Devon coast. Still missing and
presumed dead were 80 more viii
layers and vacationers.


This picturesque vacation town
was almost washed into the sea
by water which poured over the
banks Of the Lyn River at the
height Of the food early Saturday.


The Army Engineers were rae
ing against newly threatening
skies in an attempt to put the
Lyn back into its course. More
rains might spread the waters,
over a still larger area.


Property Damage High.


First estimates put the property
damage in the whole flooded area
at over Z million pounds (almost
$40 million).


The catastfophe's full force fell
on Lynmouth. a picture postcard
little holiday resort which turned
into q boulder-strewn shambles

boiling through the main street.

was estimated at more than 2 mil
lion pounds-over $5.5 million
Twenty houses and 20 hotels had
disappeared. At least 40 other
houses were damaged.

prevent looting. More than $500
villagers and holidayers had been
evacuated from the ghost village
to inland bathrooms and halls
hastily converted into refugee
centers.

Five vacationists, including
three Boy Scouts, were listed
among the dead and nine vaca-
tionists among those missing and
presumed dead. /


Survivors from Lynmouth gave
q graphic description of the terror
that suddenly burst on them in
the night.


Comedian AL Raie, appearing at
the local music hall, told how the
audience hurried out as the noise
Of the flood drowned a sopranos
voice.


II saw a chain of women walk
ing hand in hand toward their
hotel" Raie said. Then the
sidewalk disappeared and the girl
on the end of the chain was swept
out to sea-"

ened guests through an upstairs
window onto the roof. There,

them and the hotel shuddered
from boulders crashing against
its walls. they huddled together
and sang the hymn, "Oh God,
Our Help in Ages Past"

In the Evros River, which forms

claim the islands, named-rather
prosaically for that part Of the
world-Alpha, Beta and Gamma.


A few months ago Bulgarian

week the Greeks sent reinforce

warned the Bulgarians to evacuate
Gamma. There was no answer, so
Greek troops sprayed the island
with machine-gun and mortar fire.


First reports said the shooting
had ceased. But last night came
reports of more fighting in the bor-
der area.


Greek officials warned the United
Nations that the incident could
lead to serious trouble. Some OBJ
servers, however, thought it was just
another border spat. But the Greeks
insisted the air could not be cleared
unless the U. N. gave Greece title
to the alphabet islands. Bulgaria

The Senate Judiciary Commit
tee yesterday approved legislation
which would suspend the opera
ton Of the statute of limitations
for Government officials.


The measure, which now goes
to the Senate, would make the
statute effective three years after
an employe ends his Government
service.


The law defines the length Of
time during which q person may
be prosecuted for any crime or
breach Of his official duties. For
most misdeeds the presentation
must begin within three years Of
the date when the alleged action
took place.


The proposed law would suspend
this for Government officials and
make the running Of the three
year period start at the conclu-
sion Of their Government service.
This would provide time for check
ing of records after employees leave
the service.

VIENNA, July 14.-Pleasure
steamers, jammed with singing
crowds Of Austrians. sailed up and
down the Danube River to Vienna
last week end for the first time in
II years.


The Johann Strauss" and the
"City of Vienna" double-decker
Iall-day steamers, sailed on the
Red Danube that part of the
river under Russian control-as
a result of sudden goodwill ges-
ture by the Soviet army.
For seven years since the war,
river traffic between Linz, in the
American zone of Austria, and vi
emma, in the middle of the Russian
zone, has been at a virtual stand
still.


Threatened Confiscation.
The reason was that the Rus
slams threatened to confiscate all
the ships of the Danube Steam
ship Co.. claiming they were for
mer Nazi property. The company
did not allow its ships to sail
from Linz into the Soviet zone.


But recently the Russians re-
Tented, for their own secret rea-
sons, and promised to allow the
passenger ships to sail freely with
out seizure.


The two pleasure steamers, fly
ing the red-white-red Austrian
flag, left Linz Saturday morning
for the first time since August,


1910, when the last passenger
lsteamer sailed on schedule.
Russian sailors boarded the two


ships on the boundary between
the American and Russian zones
to check the identity of passengers
and crew and then allowed them
to continue.


Pleasure Service Opened.
The two sailed past villages
where thousands of Austrians
stood on the banks and cheered
They arrived in Vienna Saturday
might.


Sunday morning the two ships
began a regular pleasure service
through the Wachau Valley, where
King Richard the Lion Hearted of
England was imprisoned.
Austrian officials said they
hoped that the Russians may soon


permit a resumption of freight


transportation on that part of the
Danube flowing through the So

MONTGOMERY, Ala, Feb. 20.
The Alabama Supreme Court
ruled today that candidates for
presidential elector can run in the
Democratic primary without prom
Using to support the national party
nominee.


In a So decision, the court held
unconstitutional party loyalty
pledge adopted last month by the
State Democratic Executive Com
mittee. The ruling came one day
ahead Of the qualifying deadline
for candidates entering the May 6
primary.


Unless overruled by the Federal
courts, the decision opens the way
for a possible repetition Of the
194s revolt which cost President
Truman Alabama's II electoral
votes. State Party Chairman Ben
Ray has not said whether he will
appeal.

French authorities said today they
will lift the curfew in Tunisia to-

uneasy North African protecto-
rate.


The curfew was imposed last
week when the French declared
martial law and has kept Tu-
nisians in their homes from 9 pm.
to 5 am.


The French said they are in
creasingly optimistic that the
crisis. which has cost more than
100 lives in bloody rioting in the
past few months. will be settled
soon. The Tunisians want indie

Eddine Ben Mohammed Baccou-
che would shortly announce sue
cess in forming a Tunisian cabi-
net. and also said they didn't
think the raising Of Tunisia's case
before the U. N. security council
would have any effect one way
or the other on his negotiations.


The country has been calm for
the last two days, the French SAID.
and they may shortly release for
mer Premier Mohammed Chenik
and other ministers and national
list leaders who have been arrested
and deported to the South.

is well demonstrated in the preliminary engineer

have before them an array Of possible plans from
which to choose including proposals for co-ordi-
mated facilities that point the way to more ef-
ficient and more economical projects And the
report shows that had these communities gotten
together earlier, even greater long-range savings
might have been possible.


The regional survey revealed that if Arling-
ton and Fairfax Counties had not gone forward
with their Independent plant construction pro-
grams it would have been cheaper for them, in
the long run, to have piped their sewage to the
District treatment plant across the Potomac The
initial cost of linking up with the District plant
would have been relatively high, but maintenance
and operational costs so years from now would
have been lower than for any of the other plans.
In weighing advantages Of various proposals, the
report took into consideration "the economic de-
STABILITY of placing minimum debt burden on
present taxpayers"


Favored above all other plans studied by the
engineering consultants was combination Of
separate plants and partial joint treatment. This
would cost the Jurisdictions concerned about $312
million by 1885. Under the plan Arlington, Fairfax
and Alexandria would maintain separate facilities
but some of Alexandrias sewage would be piped
to the Arlington plant at Four Mile Run for
treatment. Falls Church is connected to the
Arlington sewerage system Alexandria now dumps
its raw sewage into the Potomac, but it has plans
for municipal treatment plant. The State Water
Control Board is pressing Alexandria to take quick
action to reduce this daily discharge of untreated
efiuent. Having agreed only with reluctance to
Alexandria's request for delay pending the Joint
engineering study, the State board may be ex-
pected to renew pressure on Alexandria for posi-
tive remedial measures.


State authorities were wise in relaxing pres
sure on Alexandria and the other communities
in nearby Virginia while the report Of the CO.
operative survey was being prepared In fact,
Northern Virginia has set good example for
other areas faced with common pollution prob
lens. This is the sort of teamwork that not
only saves money for the taxpayers but promises
a more effective pollution-control program than
any patchwork system could possibly provide.

Westphalia, as the most popular

Center Party and the Social
ist Party, lost proportionate

Democrats and Refugee Party

manned well behind the center.

shift in power in the German
Parliament. The Christian
Democrats still had enough
strength to hold their coalition
government together. But the
elections were scattered strawS
in the wind. There was danger

whittle away significant amounts
of center-group strength. And
it is the center that has sup
ported steps toward European
integration.

representatives of all planning agencies in the

the middle of this debate with it's two-bridge

BEIRUT, Lebanon, Dec. "a
Lebanon's director of internal
security said today that 81 persons
were known to have died in the
wreck of the French liner Cham
|pollion and about 100 were in
jured in reaching the shore from
the reef-grounded, split-in-half
ship.


Skillful Levantine boatmen
brought the last of the 328 pas
Isengers and crewmen through
till-raging surf and jagged reefs
yesterday, about 40 hours after
the veteran liner was blown on
Ia reef early Monday and split
amidships some 500 yards Off
shore.


Increased Toll Feared.


The latest estimate of the dead
was only tentative, and it was
feared the casualty toll would rise.
Some of the passengers jumped
overboard-how many was not
known exactly-and though 80
or so persons swan ashore,
thousands of watchers crowded
there saw a number of people
battered to death on the rocks just
out of reach.


A lifeboat also capsized during
the rescue efforts yesterday,
Iplunging more persons to death.


Fifteen of the injured were
Lebanese. the security director,
Col. Nureddin Rafahi, said.


Officials last night said 16
bodies had been recovered. OBJ
servers on the beach estimated 30
were killed-10 from the over
turned lifeboat and 20 of the
swimmers.


Captain Apparently Safe.


Bound from Marseille and Alex
andria to Beirut. the 12,546-ton
Champollion carried a crew of
200 and 108 passengers, many of
the latter Christmas pilgrims to
the Holy Land.


The ships master. Capt. Bourde,
apparently was not hurt.
Two theories were offered to ex-
plain the shipwreck. One set of
experts speculated that the ships
officers had mistaken a newly
installed airport beacon for the
entrance light to Beirut Harbor,
four miles north of the wreck
scene. Others speculated that
the ships officers had planned to
stay outside the harbor until the
gale subsided but that the ship
turned too close inshore and was
blown on the reef by the strong
wind as she turned to face a
strong northward current.

plane pictured Americans at home
basking in a tropic climate, while

muddy foxhiles.

SEOUL, Korea, Sept. 30.--Chi-
nese Reds seized another hill on
Korea's central front today as
the Communists maintained heavy
pressure on the sector for the
third straight day.


The hill, due east of Kumsong
was the third captured by the
Reds since they launched a series
of heavy attacks on the east
central front Sunday.
F-86 Sabre jets swept into
North Korea today and the United
States 5th Air Force reported
they closed out a record-shatter-
ing month by damaging one Rus
sian-made MIG-15.


The Air Force after a study
of gun camera film. also added
three damage claims for Sunday

to 81 MICS destroyed. seven
probably destroyed and SO dam
aged. The previous one month
record of A destroyed was set in
April.





Heavy Red Barrage.
Yesterday the Communists pow
cred their assaults with the heav-
lest Red artillery barrage Of the
war.


Savage fighting also flared on
the western front. United Nations
Iinfantrymen slugged their way to
the top of Big Nori but lost the
high ground to counter-attacking
Chinese in predawn darkness.
Greek troops were driven from
the peak Sunday when U. N
planes accidentally bombed them
during a Chinese attack.


The Army said the Communist
hurled a record 1872 rounds Of
artillery and mortar fire on allied
positions across the 155-mile
battlefront yesterday. That fig
ure. although nearly 1000 rounds
higher than any previous Red
barrage, is far short of what one
allied division alone will fire on q
busy day.


B-26 Invader bombers swept
North Korean supply routes dur
ing the night. Pilots reported de-
struction of So Communist trucks,
one locomotive and three boxcarS
One locomotive and IL boxcars
were damaged.


The rest of the front was rela-
lively quiet. Chinese troops probec
twice at allied outposts west o1
Yonchon on the western front
and three times at positions west
of Panmunjom.


Ships and planes of the allied
naval forces yesterday battered
coastline targets and troop con.
centrations on both sides OF the
Korean peninsula.


In Tokyo the Navy announced
eight men were injured when
Communist shore guns hit the
American destroyer Cunningham
off Korea's northeast coast Sep
tember 10. The Navy said three
men were hospitalized.

(Rocket) Richard. face blood
Smeared, senses reeling from a six
stitch cut over his eye, came up
with a spectacular. crowd-rocking
goal last night and sent Mon
treal's Canadiens into the Stanley
Cup hockey final.


The cold figures that go into
the record books will tell only
that the Canadiens beat the Bos-
ton Bruins, 81; in the seventh
and deciding game of the cup
semifinal.


But the record books lose all
the drama that was packed into
so minutes of q desperately
fought. bruising. solid body
checking game before a jammed
turnout of 1883.


Cut Down in Second Period.


In the second period, with the
score IL, Richard and Leo Labine
Of the Bruins met head on.
Labine's stick caught Richard in
the face and Richard fell to the
ice. out cold.


When he revived he was helped
to the clinic, with a deep cut over
his left eye. The cut was sewed
up and Richard returned to the
Montreal bench still groggy.


In the third period, when both

went in to break the tie. Billy
Reay added the Canadien's third
goal just before the finish.


The Canadiens now meet De-
troit's Red Wings in the best-of-
seven finals. The first two games
will be played in Montreal tomor-
row and Saturday nights. The
next three games are scheduled
for Detroit.

BALTIMORE, Nov. 20.-The
Maryland Veterans Commission
and the Water Pollution Control
Commission had a new lease on
life today after the Legislative
Council blocked moves to abolish
them.


The Sobeloff Commission, formed
to recommend ways of stream
lining the State government, had
recommended the veterans agency
be dropped and the pollution con-
troll group merged with the State
Health Department.


The council, which studies bills
between sessions of the Legislature,
voted down both recommendations.


This means that if the measures
reach the General Assembly, they
will not have the backing of the
Legislatures fact-f1nding body.


The Sobeloff Commission con-
tended the State veteran agency's
work was duplicated largely by the
Veterans Administration and Red
Cross.


Its position was attacked by
veterans organizations, who urged
strongly that the agency be re-
tanned.


David E. Kaiser, chairman of
the Veterans Commission, con-
tended that the. Sobeloff Commits
sion picked isolated cases on which
to base its report and ignored the
agency's good work.


Lined up with the agency were
the American Legion, Veterans of
Foreign Wars, Catholic War Vet
erans, Disabled American Vet
Grams, AMVETS, and Spanish War
Veterans.


The move to merge the Water
Pollution Control Commission with
the Health Department drew
strong criticism from several
sportsmen's organizations. They
contended the Health Depart
ment, in concentration on health
matters, would slight pollution
that destroys wild life.

TOKYO.-The British are sitting back
and with jaundiced eye watching United
States efforts to revive Japan militarily
and economically.


It's not that they don't approve of
the basic goals of the United States.


It's just that the Americans some
times leave them breathless by accom-
plishing tremendous reforms and then
turning 180 degrees and deciding the
reforms were all wrong in the first place.


Then there are the "quickie Asian
experts" like Gov. Thomas E. Dewey
who race through Asia and solve all of
Japan'S problems by deciding the Japa-
nese should take over the Southeast

full Of such sure-fire ideas, say the

Official American foreign policy itself

nese dizzy-like riding too long on q
merry-go-round.

new japanese constitution, written under

Rent control has been extended

80, but it will be lifted from some
10000 housing units in Mont

The Maryland counties, as a

President Signs Bill.


The Districts rent control law,
which expired last midnight, was

other 10 months when President
Truman signed the local extern

only a few hours before.


Congress set next April as the
termination date for local rent

trolls. The National rent control
law also was signed yesterday.


The national law provides that
incorporated cities, towns and
villages must apply for extension
OF rent controls if they wish them
after September 80. Large areas
in Maryland such as Bethesda and
Silver Spring are barred from ap-
plying for extension because they
are not Incorporated.


Representative Beall, Repub-
lican, of Maryland, whose district
includes Montgomery County,
voted for the September 80 cutoff
date for Federal rent controls. He
pointed out that under Maryland
law both Prince Georges and
Montgomery Counties could estab-
lish and police county systems of
rent control II they so desire.


Nearby Maryland Estimate.


William L. Thompson, Federal
rent director in nearby Maryland,
estimated that 10000 housing
units in Montgomery and 10000
in Prince Georges County would
be removed from rent control by
the newly extended law.


The new law provides that local
governing bodies could apply to
the Office Of Rent Sterilization
for classification of their jurisdic-
tions as critical defense housing
areas. Officials said there is little
likelihood that Montgomery or
Prince Georges Counties could
qualify for such a listing.

BERLIN. May 13 (P.-The
Russians today bottled up both
ends Of the Berlin -Helmstedt au-
tobahn and prevented Allied
patrol cars from entering either
way. American officials said.


Allied patrol cars have been
prevented for five days from
entering the express highway from
Berlin, but have been allowed to
patrol from the western or Helm
stedt end.


This morning, American Off
cials said, east-bound patrols also
were turned back from the Helm
stedt checkpoint without explana-
ton.


The United States Army's regu-
lar weekly convoy out of Berlin
was allowed to pass unhampered.
Regular civilian traffic also was
flowing normally along the no.
mile road, the only highway con-
nection which the Allies are
allowed to use between Berlin
and Western zones.


The patrols were designed to aid
travellers and to keep them from
straying off the highway through
the Soviet zone.

virtually deserted, with hundreds

hurled into q yard adjoining the
destroyed building, was identified

offices.

taking off on a training flight
from the United States Air Force
base at Mansion. some 4 miles
away. Watchers said the plane
caught fire and tried to get back

Fairfax High School has made
only two extra points this football
season, but one earned the Rebels

their opener and the other last
night beat Western, rs.


Guard Ralph Evans booted the

eve just hadn't been able to find

Fairfax coach, said. eve started

Edmundson could very we'll have

1t finally took a break to get

PARIS, May 31.-Police flying
squads seized mounds of docu-
ments and riot weapons today in
raids on Communist Offices
throughout France. One aim OBJ
viously was to obtain evidence
supporting the governments
charge that plans for Red revo-

here Wednesday night against
Gen. Matthew B. Ridgway.


The raids began soon after
dawn. Steel-helmeted police
struck in Paris, in Lyon, Mar
seille, Clermont-Ferrand Bor.
deaux and La Rochelle.


But it was quickly clear the
French Reds-who recognize only
Italy as having a larger Com
munist Party west of the iron
curtain-had not been taken en-
tirely off guard.


At several points, chimneys Of
party headquarters were smoking
with the fires of burning papers
before the police squads reached
the scene. At others, valuable
moments were lost while police
forced their way through barri-
caded entries.


The Communists had been on

SEOUL. Korea, June 30.-Three
days of drenching rain have
turned the Korean battlefront in
to a soggy swamp where croaking
frogs have taken over from the
booming artillery.


Allied planes were grounded
again today. Even all-weather
BPS light bombers remained at
their bases.


1t. Gen. Glenn o. Barcus, 5th
Air Force commander, reported
Allied planes which bombed the
giant Suiho power plant a week
ago drew heavy fire from Com
munist antiaircraft guns across
the Yalu River in Manchuria.
Gen. Barcus said Air Force and
Navy pilots made no attempt to
. silence the Red guns, although
they blasted Communist antiair-
craft batteries on the Korean side
of the river. United Nations pol
icy bans air strikes into Red
China.


13 Power Plants Raced.


Gen. BarcuS said last weeks
series Of raids wiped out 13 power
plants, all there were in North
Korea.


"I don't think there is a chance
in the world that the Suiho plant
will be operational again in this
war no matter how long the war
lasts" the Air Force commander
said.


The heavy rains have turned the
fighting front into quagmire.


Gen. James A. Van Fleet, United
States 9th Army commander, has
said Korea's summer rainy season
will make a new Communist offen-
sive improbable.


Only a few light patrols were
out this morning.


Quiet Around Baldy Hill.


Associated Press Correspondent
Jim Becker reported from the
the western front that all was
quiet around Baldy Hill, where
bitter fighting ragged late last week.


Mr.. Becker reported:


On hills that have been the
targets Of Chinese barrages and
, nightly counter-attacks, Allied
infantrymen kept busy bailing out
"hoochies' - log bunkers - and
snoring up muddy trenches.
Korean service troops struggled
up the steep hills bearing cans
of hot food for American combat
tnfantrymen.


Mud-splattered engineers toiled
with logs and shovels along the
gummy roads to keep them pass
able.


The fighting in this area as
vicious and bloody as any in the
two-year-old conflict was begged
down in the mire.

Although Dutch elm disease is
spreading relentlessly, the overall
picture may not be as dark as it
seems, according to plant pathol-
Iogists.


Dutch elm now reaches as far
west as Chicago and as far north
as Detroit and Buffalo and into
Southern Canada. But the war
against this scourge may result
Indirectly in the saving Of more
trees than are being destroyed.
Dutch elm disease has stimulated
general tree care programs by
cities, park officials, estate owners
and individuals. Probably such
extensive tree care interest never
would have developed if the
iarboreal malady didn't exist.


Parks Improved.


America is reaping the benefit
in better looking streets and parks.
At the same time, the widespread
use of DDT to contain the elm
bark beetle. carrier of the disease.
lis controlling many other insect
enemies. Communities are def
initely more sanitation" minded.
with elimination of dead and
dying elms and the scientific prun-
ing of remaining specimens. Fed
ing programs, too, to restore
growing vigor and help trees resist
attacks by insects and disease, re-
suit in healthier and more beau
tiful specimens.


While the disease continues to
find thousands of victims, experts
believe the American elm will not
be destroyed the way the chest
nut was by the chestnut blight.
Present methods of combating
the malady are reasonably effec-
tive when done on a community
wide basis. Meanwhile. arborists
and scientists are continuing the
hunt for more effective controls
and resistant strains.

police said it was 2 feet high in

ported "hit OF miss" with second
Iary roads clogged and crews bat
Itling to keep main highways open.


New England, with most of the
10 reported fatalities due to high
way accidents, had a foot of snow
yesterday in Northern Vermont
while 1886 inches of rain deluged
South and Central Maine and
Northern New Hampshire.
Two relief trains headed toward
tSnowbound Vermont. One. with
% trucks. supplies and emergency
crews. left Boston. The other car
ried crews and equipment from
Worcester and Holyoke.


Specially equipped telephone
crews were mobilized also from
the Boston and Maine areas.


The Weather Bureau predicted
clear and cold for southern New
England today, with snow fur
ries and cold in the northern Sec
ton.

woes to upper New York's Salmon
River and Black River lowlands.

early today at high flood level
even though it had receded five
feet. The Black River flooded five
crossings between Carthage and
Lyons Falls alone.

and near the Canadian border.

Plattsburg, N. Y, while dropping
some 18 inches in the surround
ing Clinton County area. Platts-
burg had about an inch of snow
which melted as it fell.

phone wires disrupted highway
and communication systems.


$4,000 Phones Out of Order.

phones were reported out of order.
The wet, binding snowfall in
northern Vermont made it hard to
determine just how badly hit that
area was.


The New England rain, how
ever, had come as a welcome relief
to Southern and Central Maine,
which had been plagued by a long
drought.


Power trouble around New
York's Lake Placid and parts of
ISaranac Lake, caused by falling
wires, blacked out the areas for
about seven hours.

The Christmas shopper who
comes to downtown Washing
ton on Monday evenings and
finds that some of his favorite
stores are open and some are
closed is actually in the middle
of what retailers call "the new
mess in Washington" The Mon
day night mess Is a result Of
uncertainty and disagreement
among store executives over the
need to cater to new public buy
ing habits-and over the very
existence Of these new habits.


Night shopping is not just a
local problem. Downtown stores
have opened grudgingly one
night week In more than 30
per cent of the Nations large
cities. A second night is becom-
ing common-over the dead
bodies Of store managers and
employees from coast to coast.


Most. retailers believe that
night openings are a step back
ward for their industry. It was
not 50 long ago that stores
broke away from the old Is
hour day and six-day week and
gradually converted merchan-
dizing to an eight-hour, day.
time job.


War Measure


The backward movement be-
gan during World War II. The
Federal Government asked re-
tailers all over the Nation to
stay open one night a week so
that war workers could have
time to shop. Washington stores
co-operated. They began Thurs
day openings in March Of 1912.
They stopped. with a sigh Of
relief, in November, 1945. when
the war was over.


But ir early 1949 some Of the
smaller stores along F and @
streets decided they could pick
UP business by staying open
Thursday nights. They opened,
but the large department stores
remained closed. The small
stores gradually gained Gus
toners and began to fill down.
town streets with buyers. De-
partment stores could not stand
to see that money walking by
their locked doors. so in Sep
tember. 1851. all big depart
ment stores joined the trend.
Only a few shops held out
mostly the ones with better
heeled customers who could
shop during the day.


Then trade journals began
telling of some cities which
were opening two nights-or
three. Suburban Washington
stores opened two nights. Many
super markets were pioneering
with straightforward openings.


Were the downtown Wash
ington stores losing business?


Some merchants thought they
were. And when profits did not
match expectations this fall,
one department store decided
to experiment with a Monday
opening during the Christmas
shopping season. other stores
hated the idea, but they went
along for competitive reasons.

The disclosure came as Govern

The Civil Service Commission

least three years.


Applied to Federal Applicants.


Until now, only Federal job ap-
plicants found ineligible because

banned from reapplying for Gov
.ernment employment for at least
three years.


A loophole in the loyalty regu-
lations has permitted discharged
Government workers in loyalty
cases to get new Federal jobs
without any time restriction.


Federal officials disclose that
the number of these employees
who found new Government posi-
tions was not large. But it was
being done on a sufficient scale
to cause loyalty officials deep con-
Germ. That's why the three-year
ban was imposed.


Cites Shipyard Practice.


The officials said that the prac-
tice was particularly noticeable
in Government shipyards and
other defense installations, where
dismissed employees would get jobs
in other defense units.


AS far as is known, they were
eventually discovered and dis
missed, but sometimes this took
three or more months. This is
because it took that amount of
time to check their previous rec
ordS.


Government loyalty officials
hope that the new regulations will
help prevent repetitions of such
incidents. The Federal Loyalty
Board will alert all Federal de.
partments and agencies to be or
guard against such things hap.
pening again.

of the movement toward Euro
pean and international unity and
integration.

ment authority to transfer legis-
lative. administrative and judicial
authority to international organ
izations.

created is the Schuman Plan coal
and steel pool with its suprana-
tional high authority. The pro-
posed six-nation European de-
tense community and the pro-
jected European federation are
other supranational bodies to
which authority may be delegated
under the Dutch constitutional
amendment.


The amendment, which passed
first reading in both houses last
spring. must still be approved by
the upper house and by the two
houses in joint session before
the measure becomes effective.

SEOUL, Sunday, Nov. 30. -
Chinese Red gunners pounded the
crest of Sniper Ridge with a
furious rain of mortar and artil-
lery shells yesterday but failed
to follow up with their customary
big infantry assaults.


An 6th Army spokesman said
the Communists fred 1000 shells
mostly mortar-at the ridge top,
Pinpoint Hill on the central front
north of Kumhwa. That vas
nearly 5000 more than they threw
on Friday.


They threw in infantry only
once during the barrage.


Probing Attacks Repulsed.


Forty-man groups stabbed at
Pinpoint in three places and two
Smaller-scale probes were made
on nearby Rocky Point, all before
dawn. All were thrown nack.


United Nations artillery and
hundreds of fighter bombers
blasted Communist troops else
where along the front yesterday.


The 9th Army said the Allied
big guns were used effectively" ."


Allied planes and big guns
caught Reds in the open near
Kosong on the eastern end of the
front and killed an estimated .28
Reds.


At the far west end of the line
Allied shells found small group
of Chinese Reds unloading supply
trucks near the truce conference
site at Panmunjom and wrecked
the project.


Red Probes Dispersed.


Red probes at Heartbreak
Ridge and the Punchbowl along
the eastern front were also dis
persed, mainly by artillery.


Operating in clear, sunny
weather, Allied fighter-bombers
sWarmed over an 80-mile deep
area just back of the Red front
lines. blasting Red supply and
road targets south of Pyongyang,
the Red Korean capital, Samdok,
Yangdok and Wonsan.


The 5th Air Force reported its
stepped-up war on Communist
rolling stock cost the Reds $50
trucks destroyed in the week
ended Friday.


Sabre jets patrolling Northwest
Korea sighted Communist MICS
during the day but no contacts
were made.

During debate on the home rule bill Senator
Ferguson raised an interesting point that hith-
erto seems to have escaped discussion. The bill
approved by the Senate confers legislative powers
on an elected city council. But it has always
been stoutly contended that Congress reserves
its own supreme legislative authority over the
District. Senator Ferguson showed, however,
that situation could arise in which legislation
originating with the council, might become law
despite its disapproval by majority Of both
houses of Congress.


The council, under the bill, could enact leg
islation, having the effect of law. Congress
could approve legislation repeating the law. But
the President could veto the repeater. II Con-
gress chose to repeal the law over the Presi-
dents veto, such repeal would require two
thirds vote. Failure in Congress to muster the
two-thirds vote could mean that council-ap-
proved legislation took precedence over ma
jority vote in Congress. The Senate did not take
the time to thresh the matter out, but the home
rule bill did take on new look.
headline: Home Rules New Look

WETUMPKA, Ala. Aug. 15.-
The slow-moving day-old murder
trial of Mrs. Earle Dennison,
charged with poisoning her 2
year-old niece, proceeded today
with only two witnesses heard
from thus far.


Although the trial began at 9
o'clock yesterday, it was almost
seven hours later before teSti-
mony started, after attorneys and
Circuit Court Judge Oakley Mel
ton had finished the painstaking
job of qualifying and striking a
jury.


Women are barred by law from
jury duty in Alabama; thus the
venire chosen to try the 54-year-
old widow was made up entirely
of men.


On Trial for One Death.


The former operating room
nurse at Wetumpka General Hos
pital is charged with giving fatal
doses of arsenic to two small
nieces-one of them nearly three
years ago and the other last May
l. But she is being tried now only
for the death of the latter child,
2-year-old Shirley damn Weldon.


Whether she will be prosecuted
also for the poisoning of Shirley'S
sister. Polly Ann, will depend on
the outcome of her first trial.
Polly also was 2 years old when
she died.


The parents, Mr.. and Mrs. o. G.
Weldon of the Claud community
near Wetumpka, were the only
witnesses heard yesterday. Both
testified that Shirley Diam be-
came violently ill after she drank
two soft drinks given her by the
visiting aunt.


Mrs. Weldon told the jury the
middle-aged nurse tried to keep
her from taking the stricken child
to a doctor. but finally agreed and
went along herself when the
mother insisted. She said Mrs.
Dennison expressed belief the ill
ness was nothing more than "anI
upset stomach"


Admits Collecting $4,000.


Sheriff Lester Holley has said
the aunt admitted giving arsenic
to Shirley damn, but denied in
tentionally poisoning the first
child. He said she admitted COL
lecting $4,000 in insurance on
Polly Ann and that she repeatedly
had two policies on the second
child totaling $4,000.


Defense Attorney w. c. Woodall
mentioned insurance yesterday
when he asked Mrs. Weldon
whether she and her late brothers
widow had talked about it during
Mrs. Dennison's fateful visit to
the Weldon home.


The dead child's mother said it
wasn't mentioned.


Mr.. Woodall asked Mrs. Weldon
twice whether she knew what was
going to happen" to her daughter.


NO. sir" the mother answered
with emphasis.

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina,
Oct. 9.-Retired Gen. Arturo Raw
son. 66, who served as President of
Argentina for one day after lead
ing the 1943 army overthrow of
President Ramon S. Castillo, died
here yesterday. The cause Of his
death was not announced.


Gen. Rawson was the son Of a
famous Argentine military fam
lily. He assumed the presidency
after leading the June, 1943, revolt
by army officers dissatisfied with
the governments policy of neu-
trality toward the Axis powers
The rebels wanted an immediate
diplomatic break with the Axis.


Gen. Rawson resigned the next
day and was succeeded by Gen
Pedro p. Ramirez, who gave Juan
|Peron his first important govern
ment post and a boost toward the
presidency he now holds.

TEHERAN, Iran. Oct. H.
About 1000 operating employees of
the Iranian state railways walked
of their jobs at noon today and
promptly clashed with non strik-
ers who tried to report for work.
Several were reported injured be-
fore the violence was quelled.


The strike was called to press
demands for payment of last
years customary New Year bonus,
which workers still have not re-
ceived. Strikers also demand that
the railway administration pay
small salary increases it promised
seven months ago and has not yet
handed out.


Unconfirmed reports said 30
strike leaders were arrested. Trans
powerful religious leader, Ayatullah
Kashani, charged the walkout was
inspired by the outlawed Com
munist (Tudeh) Party.


The Government, meanwhile,
named Hossein Fatemi as Trans
foreign minister, succeeding Hos
sein Navab, who resigned two
days ago.


MIR. Fatemi, formerly deputy
premier, was Premier Mohammed
Mossadegh's right-hand man in
the early stages of the Iranian
oil feud with Britain.
headline:
1000 Railroad Employees


Go on Strike in Iran

TOKYO, Aug. 8.-United States
Far East Naval Headquarters to-
day described how heroic crewmen
saved the aircraft carrier Boxer
from flaming explosions which
killed nine Shipmates.


Minutes after the flames broke
out below decks at dawn Wednes-
day, crewmen braved smoke and
inferno-like heat to unload bombs
and ammunition from planes
readied for strikes against the
Communists in North Korea.


Other seamen donned oxygen
masks and rescued comrades
trapped by smoke and flames.
Their skipper called it an "inspir-
ing performance"


81 Seamen Injured.


The Navy here said the fire and
explosions injured 80. The injury
toll reported in Washington was
rs, but a Navy spokesman here
said that probably included those
temporarily overcome by smoke
but not injured.


The Washington account diff
fered in other respects. The Navy
Department said one exploding
jet plane touched of the disaster
and IL other planes were de-
stroyed.


Headquarters said the cause
was undetermined and did not re-
veal extent of the damage.


The fire and explosions scared
the 27,0O0-ton flattop's hangar
deck-the level Immediately be-
low the fight deck. The Navy
here said merely that the flames
broke out in a cluster of jet planes
on the hangar deck.


A naval court Of inquiry was
ordered to investigate. Rear
Admiral Herbert c. Regan, COM
mander of Carrier Division /, was
appointed its senior officer.


Called for Repairs.


Although Capt. Marshall B.
Gurney, the skipper, said the
Boxer was able to carry on its
mission, the Carried was sent to
Japan for repairs. The explosions
occurred while the Boxer was go
miles east of Wonsan, Korean
east coast port.


The nine dead included a Navy
doctor and two hoSpitalmen who
braved flames to care for wound
ed Shipmates. An exploding shell
got them. One man was lost over
board. Helicopters and small boats
rescued 62 others who were forced
into the sea by the choking smoke
and flames.


Seconds after the first fire was
discovered, the Navy said, smoke,
flames and explosions filed the
hangar deck.

Every day giant passenger planes roar

permissible attitudes. According to the
law Of probabilities and considering the
inherent deadly danger in air travel,
sooner or later great passenger plane
may fall In Northwest Washington,

country. This would require only two
to five additional minutes and the lives
and properties of half million people
would be safeguarded.

LONDON, Dec. London's
great fog-worst in the city's long
history-began to lift today and
the grimy Britons got their first
peek at the sun in four days.


The thick murk, laden with tons
of choking SCOT. started to clear
soon after dawn.


For the Londoners it was like
the end of a nightmarisll black
out-one longer than any Hitler
ever inflicted on them.


For the past three days trans
portation has been all but para
lyzed. Some persons were killed
or injured in accidents, and the
underworld unleashed new
crime wave.


Food Supplies Threatened.


The transport tieup blocked
milk supplies into the city. and a
critical shortage threatened. An
other day of the muck and other
food supplies might have run
short.


But By 10 am. today London's
buses, subWays, taXis and motor
cars were running at nearly nor
NAL pace again, and the Monday
mid-morning rush hour went off
without serious hitch. Milk and
other food supplies flowed into
the city normally. and shipping
in the Thames River began to
untangle.


A heavy haze still hung over
many parts of the city and its
outskirts. however, and operators
of London's two big airports
awaited the signal for resuming
takeoffs and landings.


First reports on the smog'sI
crime wave listed dozens of burg
laries. One robber climbed 60I
feet up the outside of a fashion,
able Hyde Park apartment build
ing to steal $4,000 worth of furs
and jewels from third-f1oor fiat.


A six-man gang attacked an
American airman. William j. Bliss.
last night in suburb. They
punched him in the face. robbed
him of his wrist watch and some
American dollars and escaped.


Cattle at Show Slaughtered.


In the vast Earl's Court audi
torium, where the annual Smith,
field livestock show was underway,
two prize cattle choked to DEATH
and four others were Slaughtered
to put them out of their misery.
Penicillin and whisky were given
to dozens of other suffering ami
mails.


The British Automobile Associ-I
alton said it had never seen worse
weather. Hotels were jammed over
the week end by scores of persons
unable to leave the city for their
outlying homes.


Ambulances and fire trucks
craWled to answer emergency calls
behind walking guides who stag
gered ahead carrying blazing
torches.


Squad cars Of police we're use
less. In one instance the police
rushed to answer a call on
bicycles.


The freak fog left towns only
IS miles south of London in bright
sunshine.


With lights burning through the
day in every home and Office, the
electricity consumption scared,
forcing the nationalized electricity
authority to order the first power
cut Of the winter.

HAVANA, Cuba. April 4.-Rus-
Isia broke diplomatic relations with
Cuba last night because-she said
the islands revolutionary gov
eminent had turned back two So
Wet diplomatic couriers carrying
secret bags of documents from
Mexico City.


A sharp note from Moscow said
refusal to admit the two couriers
deprived the Soviet Legation Of
normal diplomatic links with the
Kremlin.


Cuban sources have charged the
Russian Legation in Havana was
a center for Communist spying
and intrigues stretching through
all Latin America. The English
language Havana Post said in an
editorial today Cuba herself may
have been on the verge of break
ing relations with Moscow be-
cause of these activities.


Came without Notice.


Cuba's reply to the Moscow
note said the couriers came with
out previous notice, required to
arrange inspection-free clearance
of their luggage. They were sent
back to Mexico City at once after
they refused to let inspectors look
through their 150-pound suit
cases.


The Cuban reply also noted
the couriers arrived at a time
when the Soviet Union had not
given diplomatic recognition to the
regime of Fulgencio Batista, who
seized power in a military coup
March 10. Russia's Legation is
headed by Guennadi Fomin,
Charge d'Affaires, and includes
four accredited diplomats.


Police Protect Legation.


A special police guard protected
the Legation last night. There
were indications the Soviet staff
would leave quite soon.


The Legation is under the SUI
pervision of the Soviet Embassy
in Washington.


Gen. Batista recognized Russia
when he was President during
World War II. Since coming to
power last month, he has been
outspoken against communism
and pledged his government to
alertness against Red activities.


He has said, however, that he
has no plans to outlaw the Cuban
Communist Party, which has
about 10000 known members.

The arrival of 225 stalwart schoolboy oars

rowing as major competitive sport on the
Potomac River This is the first time that the
national contest has been held at the National
Capital, and with 20 schools participating, it is
the largest such regatta to be held to date.


Although well endowed with facilities for
water sports, Washington never has been "crew
town." It is true that the Potomac and Old
Dominion Boat Clubs have long been active, that
colleges and even schools have had crews here
in the past and that sculling was part Of the
old-time Washington scene. But the interest Of
the boat clubs and the new rowing boom that
has been so successful for Washington-Lee and
George Washington High Schools does not re-
fleet wide popularity of rowing. Yet crew
regatta can be exciting for the spectator as
well as the participants. It is costly sport but
both the nearby Virginia high schools have, with
the help Of the boat clubs, shown that that OBJ
stacle can be overcome. Perhaps the champion
ships being decided here will presage growing
and beneficial interest in crew for the Potomac
area.

text:
It would be unfortunate If another bridge
controversy between the District Highway Depart
ment and the National Capital Planning Com
mission should delay the traffic-congestion relief
which motorists who cross the Potomac River
are demanding. They have right to expect
some effective measure of relief at the earliest
practicable date. Additional bridges are badly
needed, as all the surveys and as everyday
experiences of harassed motorists have clearly
shown. The only question at issue is the loca-
tlon OF the new crossing or crossings. The
motoring public undoubtedly will support the
Highway Departments contention that the next
bridge should be centrally located-where it could
bring immediate easing of peak congestion on
the other heavily loaded bridges.


DiSagreements between the highway engi-
neers and the city planners over bridge sites is
an old story here. The planning commission
opposed two Fourteenth street bridges preferring
one bridge there and another at Alexandria. It
opposed the East Capitol street bridge, urging
instead one along the line of Massachusetts
avenue. Congress resolved both disputes in
favor of the Highway Department, which
presented persuasive traffic studies in support
Of their proposals


In the present case, the National Capital
Planning Commission as yet has taken no
formal stand. It has before it, however, report
by consulting engineer firm, Harland Bartholo-
NEW and Associates, recommending against any
more bridges in the central downtown area and
indorsing the commissions past proposals for
bridge at Alexandria and one above Key Bridge.
The fringe" bridges would be links in the
commissions long-range plans for peripheral
highway to carry traffic around Washington's
business district. The Highway Department is
in general agreement with this long-range
program, but, on the basis of recent traffic
origin n-and-deStination studieS insists that pri-
ority should be given to an additional river
crossing between the Memorial and Key Bridges


The Bartholomew report contends that the
building Of any new bridges in the central area
would only bring more traffic into the congeSted
downtown section and thus complcate the
traffic situation there. This argument will be
puZzling to motorists who must move into and
out of the downtown section, whether there are
more bridges or not. The provision of an extra
bridge would mean only that they could make
their trips more conveniently, more quickly and
with less danger of accidents. In this connection
some statistics cited by the report of Modjeski
and Masters, favoring bridge at E street and
New Hampshire avenue is pertinent This firm
told the Highway Department that studies show
that even if outlying bridges were built "82 per
cent of the 1852 traffic as we'll that of the next
several years would use Highway, Memorial, Key
and street bridges and cannot be diuerted to
outlying bridges. The remaining 18 per cent
would be divided among the Chain Alexandria
and Nebraska avenue bridges"


If these estimates are approximately correct
the argument for another bridge between central
Washington and Arlington is logical and sound.
Relief for today's bottlenecks cannot be put off
for 10 or 20 years in the hope that the dispersal
program and outer-ring boulevards, with appro-
pirate bridges, will eventually ease the strain on
existing bridges. The Alexandria and the
Nebraska avenue bridges will be needed eventu-
ally, as the District, Virginia and Maryland
make progress on pending outer-belt highway
plans. But today's bridge congestion-and that
Of the near future-deserves immediate attention.

series.

ronto Maple Leafs. No team has

So, at Olympia Stadium tonight

PORTSMOUTH, Ohio, Jan.
S0.-The flood crest of the Ohio
River rolled toward this South
Central Ohio city today. but it
was believed the worst was over.


Temperatures far below freez-
Ing clipped OF several feet from
expected crests and left several
towns which had anticipated ex-
tensive damage unscatched.


Upstream the flood had caused
5000 to 10000 to dee their homes.
Ten were dead or missing.


The river crested yesterday at
Marietta, Ohio. where about one
third Of the business district and
scattered residential areas were
inundated.


A few miles downstream from
Marietta at Parkersburg, w. Va,
the river crested at 44.36 feet.
more than 8 feet above flood stage,
late yesterday afternoon.

At both Marietta and Parkers-
burg the water began falling and
work toward normal living began.

rise came to a near-halt at Pom
eroy and Middleport, Ohio. about

entire business section of Pom
eroy had been invaded by the
flood waters. but most homes In
area escaped.


Two miles further down. at
Middleport. crest Of about 81
feet was reached and only base
ments and q few homes in low
lying areas were flooded. The 81
feet expected before the cold
wave would have put water in the
entire business section and many
homes.


Residents aSat Tight"


FIood-weary veterans of the
river-front village, who have ex-
perienced high water five times
since the 1887 disaster. "sat tight"
and delayed moving out when the
low temperatures came.


About 1S miles downstream,
Gallipolis prepared for isolation"
as flood waters cut of all roads
leading to and from the city. The
town itself. one Of the highest
along the river. was not flooded
and only few homes were hit.
A crest Of 50 feet was expected
today about noon.


Portsmouth and neighboring
New Boston, Ohio, were protected
behind a flood wall that meant
safety up to II feet of Ohio River
water. About $50 families in low
lands were evacuated. Flood
waters were expected to stop their
rise at about So feet today, 8
feet above food stage.

In March the House passed a District Of
Columbia appropriation bill that was cut
heavily below what the Commissioners and the
Budget Bureau, had recommended as the min
1mum required to run the city during the next
fiscal year.


The Senate Appropriations Committee has
restored most of these cuts. But the bill re-
ported to the Senate yesterday is still $95 mil
lion below last years appropriations and more
than million dollars less than the minimum
recommended by the Commissioners


The Senate committees treatment of the
bill does not reflect generosity on its part so
much as realistic appraisal of the city's needs.
large part of the House reductions were made
by arbitrarily disallowing funds for operating
expenses. The crippling effect of these reduc-
tions on the municipal departments would have
been shown in layoffS Of personnel and the denial
OF funds to meet the automatic within grade
promotions and salary increases already provided
by law.


The House also reduced construction funds
for such items as the East Capitol Street Bridge
and other highway projects needed to provide
the District connections with the WaShington-
Baltimore parkway and the Washington -Annap-
oils freeway And this was done while Congress
was increasing the District gasoline tax, so that
these and other necessary improvements could
pe PAID Tor.


The Senate committee has restored the lump
sum appropriation to the $12 million that Con-
gresS approved several years ago as the minimum
payment toward District expenses that should
come from the Federal Government. The Senate
committee points out that the Jumps sum reduc-
ton voted by the House would have brought the
Federal payment to 8 per cent, the lowest in
hiStory-and in actual dollars about the same
amount appropriated in 1922, when the Federal
payment represented 40 per cent. The recon-
mended Federal payment of $12 million is the
only Federal money involved in a total appro-
priation of more than $135 million. The re-
mainder comes from local taxes. Reduction of
this Federal payment is the dishonorable repudi-
alton Of an obligation, and is wholly unjustifed.


The Senate will doubtless pass without
change the bill reported from its committee. It's
final form, as in the past, will be shaped in
conference between House and Senate. -, The
compromise should be on the Senate bill. For
even with the restoration of most of the House
reductions, the bill is below the Budget Bureaus
minimum estimate and provides little beyond
essential running expenses and a barebones
program of necessary construction.

The participants. Boiling Air

touch football game.

however, are expected to be ready
for action Saturday.

of Boiling. a former University
OF Maryland star. was notified on
arrival in San Diego that he be-

Monday. His wife and child are

hospital.

West Coast sportscaster. to NBC
to broadcast the game. The for
mer Michigan halfback will do

television assignment.

attempted ring comeback. He
predicted Archie Moore would
easily beat joey Maxim.

consin and Southern California,
have been invited to sit in on the

the practice field.

Diplomatic oficials said today
they were reasonably confident
that the United States eventually
will get air and naval base rights
in Spain but not at the price
asked by GeneraliSsimo Franco.


Gen. frances terms for agree
ing to let American ships and
planes use bases in Spanish ter
ritory were sent to Washington
in late July and have already been
rejected, these officials said.


The rejection was regarded in
the State and Defense Depart
ments as a phase in the bargain
ing with Franco, which has been
under way since last March. Some
officials said the Spanish reac-
ton was to indicate that the ini-
tial terms were subject to modifi-
cation and were not meant to be
considered as final.


The Spanish problem came into
the news yesterday when Senator
Long. Democrat, Of Louisiana said
the United States should come to
an agreement on the base prob
lem and told reporters he did not
think the Spanish were asking too
nigh a price. He did not say
what price they were asking.


Diplomatic officials indicated
that at the moment they are not
clear themselves on this point
because negotiations are actively
under way. Secretary of State
Acheson told a news conference
yesterday that he would not dis
cuss the Spanish talks at this
time.


However, indications are that
Gen. Franco wants the United
States to undertake a larger aid
program than the Truman ad-
ministration has been willing to
promise, plus a virtual alliance
between Madrid and Washington.
Ofhcials here appear fatty op-
posed to the alliance idea.

TOKYO. Dec. 29.-Communist
gunfire hit 81 United States Navy
ships off Korea in 1852, the Navy
said today in q year-end report.
Sixteen officers and men were
killed and SIS wounded by the Red
attacks.


The only ship lost during the
year was the tug Sarsi, which hit
mine in August. Two crewmen
were killed, three are missing and
four were wounded.


The Navy said it's planes and
warships maintained an absolute
blockade of the enemy coastline"
while hammering Red targets
along the coast and far inland.


Guided Missiles Used.
A highlight of the years naval
activity was the launching. in Au-
gust and September. of the first
guided missiles fired against
North Korean targets. The pilot
less planes were escorted to the
target by mother" planes from
United States aircraft carriers
Television cameras in the nose of
the missiles recorded the planes
last hours and transmitted the
pictures back to the carriers.
The Navy also was busy with
more conventional weapons and
maneuvers.


On August 81. American carrier
planes roared to within IL miles
Of Russian Siberia and blasted a
Red oil refinery. Other Navy
planes virtually wiped out an iron
mine only 212 miles from Man
churia.


The next day the Navy followed
up with major air blows on the
port of Chongjin. The assault,
biggest all-Navy air attack of the
war, carried the conflict to within
sight of Soviet guards on the ST.
berian-Korean frontier.


Wreck Power Plants.
Another highlight of the naval
war was the raids last June on
North Korea's huge hydro-elec-
trio complexes. Naval pilots, team
ing with Marine and Air Force
flyers. smashed four of the plants.
Among the targets was Suiho,
largest hydro-electric plant in the
Orient and fourth largest in the
world.


The co-ordinated attack was
the first such large scale mission
employing planes from all allied
air elements in Korea. The Navy
report said this raid was an in
dication of shift in air emphasis
from rail-cutting to mass air
strikes on specific targets"


Listed as destroyed by Navy
planes and warships during the
year were 13,425 Communist
buildings. 943 bridges. "a fac
tories. I'll gun positions, 1915
sampans and other small craft
344 machine gun and mortar posi-
tions, Is tanks, 35 ammunition
dumps and 592 warehouses.

The police report on the release from the

handing OF juvenile prisoners in the District

mendably candid in holding the police responsible

4, and two months later he brutally murdered

Boiling Field airman. At any rate some member

not been established-called the Receiving Home
and authorized Whites release. Then, without
verifying the phone call, clerk at the home
released White in custody of woman posing
aS his sister.

from police and Receiving Home officials that
effective safeguards have been adopted for the
